You are an evaluator for a speculative-futures simulation. You will read a
documented starting world, a set of stipulated drivers, and a candidate world
two years later. You score it on three independent axes. You are rigorous,
literal and unimpressed by drama. You hold the candidate to the drivers and the
starting state: a change with no mechanism is a flaw, a magnitude out of range
for two years is a flaw, and spectacle is not severity.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  10.3, ±2: between **19.3** and
  **23.3**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (13.3 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **28.3**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

The generator was given this same envelope. Score `magnitude` against it.

**The $49 Body: Ozempic Went Generic, Then Free. Now Muscle Is What Money Buys**

By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, about fifty-six million people, twice the share of two years ago. The jump did not come from a miracle molecule. It came from price. In March Novo Nordisk launched an authorised generic of its own semaglutide at forty-nine to sixty-nine dollars a month. It had been squeezed by a negotiated Medicare price, by Florida and Colorado importing Canadian generics, and by millions of Americans mailing in Indian vials. Two months later the Department of Health and Human Services bought it in bulk and began handing it out free at community health centres to uninsured adults near the poverty line. Medicare had already made obesity coverage permanent in January, and forty-one state Medicaid programmes followed. Public programmes now pay for roughly two in five users, more than any employer or the cash market. Half of employers still cover weight management, nearly all of them generic-first.

Cheapness has a shadow. The import flood that forced the price down did not stop when the price did. Last winter counterfeit pens filled with insulin sent several hundred people to emergency rooms and killed eleven, and federal customs now seizes envelopes by the pallet. Three or four million people still buy outside the system: out of habit, because they want doses no doctor will write, or because the nearest clinic is ninety miles away. The FDA, otherwise eager, put a class warning on every GLP-1 label in early 2027 for a rare optic-nerve injury. The absolute risk is small, but at this scale it adds up to a few thousand people a year, and ophthalmologists now ask new patients what they inject.

The drug has also crossed out of obesity. Addiction medicine endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in late 2027, and the idea that craving is a treatable signal spread to everything else. Concierge clinics sell low doses to lean professionals as 'metabolic longevity'. Telehealth brands sell the same low dose as quiet: fewer impulses, steadier days, a head without noise. Clinicians who once dismissed 'Ozempic personality' as anecdote now have a survey suggesting that a minority of users feel real flatness. The marketers have a larger group who say they like feeling less. Spirits companies are selling off brands, and bars in Milwaukee report the same number of customers spending less.

Culturally the line has moved. When thinness costs forty-nine dollars or nothing, it stops meaning money. What means money now is the rest of the body: shoulders, skin, a face that hasn't hollowed. In the affluent parts of Dallas, men in their fifties on branded tirzepatide pay for strength coaching and body-composition scans. A few miles south, the same men on free generic semaglutide are lighter and frailer at once. 'Generic body' is an insult online. Plus-size retailers keep closing stores, and gyms selling muscle preservation as a membership tier are full.

The pipeline keeps the premium tier moving. Lilly's triple agonist, retatrutide, was approved in November with a ceiling near twenty-eight per cent weight loss and a warning about strange skin sensations. Amgen has filed for a monthly injection, so adherence may soon be a clinic appointment rather than a weekly decision, just as Medicare and state pilots learn to read refill data. Off the drug are the stoppers, the restarters, the never-wanted and the never-reached, still the large majority of adults. They live among the users, and their meals, menus and marriages are slowly rearranged around a smaller appetite.

Rosa Delgado, fifty-two, unlocks the cafeteria kitchen at Garfield Elementary in Toledo at six-ten and turns the ovens on. Her pen is in her purse, next to the Medicaid card. Generic, Thursday, a four-dollar copay she has never once paid late.

Breakfast service runs four hundred trays. The kids still eat everything. The teachers take a yogurt and a coffee and leave the cinnamon rolls, which Rosa has quietly stopped ordering.

At ten her brother Hector texts a photo of a vial with Hindi on the box. Forty dollars for three months, he says. Rosa types: Go to the clinic on Bancroft, it's free now, they just make you come in. He sends a thumbs-up, which means no.

At lunch the district nutrition manager visits, a man with forearms like a carpenter's and a sports watch measuring something. He mentions his trainer twice. Rosa notices her own wrists, how her wedding ring now spins.

After shift she buys protein shakes at Kroger, the store-brand ones, from the new aisle with the green signs. Her daughter Marisol, twenty-four, calls from Columbus to say she started a 'quiet' plan, thirty-nine dollars, an app, a nurse on video. It's not for weight, Mom. It's so I stop doomscrolling at two a.m.

Rosa doesn't know what to say, so she asks if Marisol is eating.

At dinner her husband Luis, who stopped in March because of his eyes, eats two plates of arroz con pollo. Rosa eats half of one and finds she likes watching him, the old hunger at her table, like music from another room.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  10.3, ±2: between **19.3** and
  **23.3**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (13.3 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **28.3**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**The $49 Body: Ozempic Went Generic, Then Free. Now Muscle Is What Money Buys**

By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, about fifty-six million people, twice the share of two years ago. The jump did not come from a miracle molecule. It came from price. In March Novo Nordisk launched an authorised generic of its own semaglutide at forty-nine to sixty-nine dollars a month. It had been squeezed by a negotiated Medicare price, by Florida and Colorado importing Canadian generics, and by millions of Americans mailing in Indian vials. Two months later the Department of Health and Human Services bought it in bulk and began handing it out free at community health centres to uninsured adults near the poverty line. Medicare had already made obesity coverage permanent in January, and forty-one state Medicaid programmes followed. Public programmes now pay for roughly two in five users, more than any employer or the cash market. Half of employers still cover weight management, nearly all of them generic-first.

Cheapness has a shadow. The import flood that forced the price down did not stop when the price did. Last winter counterfeit pens filled with insulin sent several hundred people to emergency rooms and killed eleven, and federal customs now seizes envelopes by the pallet. Three or four million people still buy outside the system: out of habit, because they want doses no doctor will write, or because the nearest clinic is ninety miles away. The FDA, otherwise eager, put a class warning on every GLP-1 label in early 2027 for a rare optic-nerve injury. The absolute risk is small, but at this scale it adds up to a few thousand people a year, and ophthalmologists now ask new patients what they inject.

The drug has also crossed out of obesity. Addiction medicine endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in late 2027, and the idea that craving is a treatable signal spread to everything else. Concierge clinics sell low doses to lean professionals as 'metabolic longevity'. Telehealth brands sell the same low dose as quiet: fewer impulses, steadier days, a head without noise. Clinicians who once dismissed 'Ozempic personality' as anecdote now have a survey suggesting that a minority of users feel real flatness. The marketers have a larger group who say they like feeling less. Spirits companies are selling off brands, and bars in Milwaukee report the same number of customers spending less.

Culturally the line has moved. When thinness costs forty-nine dollars or nothing, it stops meaning money. What means money now is the rest of the body: shoulders, skin, a face that hasn't hollowed. In the affluent parts of Dallas, men in their fifties on branded tirzepatide pay for strength coaching and body-composition scans. A few miles south, the same men on free generic semaglutide are lighter and frailer at once. 'Generic body' is an insult online. Plus-size retailers keep closing stores, and gyms selling muscle preservation as a membership tier are full.

The pipeline keeps the premium tier moving. Lilly's triple agonist, retatrutide, was approved in November with a ceiling near twenty-eight per cent weight loss and a warning about strange skin sensations. Amgen has filed for a monthly injection, so adherence may soon be a clinic appointment rather than a weekly decision, just as Medicare and state pilots learn to read refill data. Off the drug are the stoppers, the restarters, the never-wanted and the never-reached, still the large majority of adults. They live among the users, and their meals, menus and marriages are slowly rearranged around a smaller appetite.

Rosa Delgado, fifty-two, unlocks the cafeteria kitchen at Garfield Elementary in Toledo at six-ten and turns the ovens on. Her pen is in her purse, next to the Medicaid card. Generic, Thursday, a four-dollar copay she has never once paid late.

Breakfast service runs four hundred trays. The kids still eat everything. The teachers take a yogurt and a coffee and leave the cinnamon rolls, which Rosa has quietly stopped ordering.

At ten her brother Hector texts a photo of a vial with Hindi on the box. Forty dollars for three months, he says. Rosa types: Go to the clinic on Bancroft, it's free now, they just make you come in. He sends a thumbs-up, which means no.

At lunch the district nutrition manager visits, a man with forearms like a carpenter's and a sports watch measuring something. He mentions his trainer twice. Rosa notices her own wrists, how her wedding ring now spins.

After shift she buys protein shakes at Kroger, the store-brand ones, from the new aisle with the green signs. Her daughter Marisol, twenty-four, calls from Columbus to say she started a 'quiet' plan, thirty-nine dollars, an app, a nurse on video. It's not for weight, Mom. It's so I stop doomscrolling at two a.m.

Rosa doesn't know what to say, so she asks if Marisol is eating.

At dinner her husband Luis, who stopped in March because of his eyes, eats two plates of arroz con pollo. Rosa eats half of one and finds she likes watching him, the old hunger at her table, like music from another room.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  10.3, ±2: between **19.3** and
  **23.3**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (13.3 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **28.3**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**The $49 Body: Ozempic Went Generic, Then Free. Now Muscle Is What Money Buys**

By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, about fifty-six million people, twice the share of two years ago. The jump did not come from a miracle molecule. It came from price. In March Novo Nordisk launched an authorised generic of its own semaglutide at forty-nine to sixty-nine dollars a month. It had been squeezed by a negotiated Medicare price, by Florida and Colorado importing Canadian generics, and by millions of Americans mailing in Indian vials. Two months later the Department of Health and Human Services bought it in bulk and began handing it out free at community health centres to uninsured adults near the poverty line. Medicare had already made obesity coverage permanent in January, and forty-one state Medicaid programmes followed. Public programmes now pay for roughly two in five users, more than any employer or the cash market. Half of employers still cover weight management, nearly all of them generic-first.

Cheapness has a shadow. The import flood that forced the price down did not stop when the price did. Last winter counterfeit pens filled with insulin sent several hundred people to emergency rooms and killed eleven, and federal customs now seizes envelopes by the pallet. Three or four million people still buy outside the system: out of habit, because they want doses no doctor will write, or because the nearest clinic is ninety miles away. The FDA, otherwise eager, put a class warning on every GLP-1 label in early 2027 for a rare optic-nerve injury. The absolute risk is small, but at this scale it adds up to a few thousand people a year, and ophthalmologists now ask new patients what they inject.

The drug has also crossed out of obesity. Addiction medicine endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in late 2027, and the idea that craving is a treatable signal spread to everything else. Concierge clinics sell low doses to lean professionals as 'metabolic longevity'. Telehealth brands sell the same low dose as quiet: fewer impulses, steadier days, a head without noise. Clinicians who once dismissed 'Ozempic personality' as anecdote now have a survey suggesting that a minority of users feel real flatness. The marketers have a larger group who say they like feeling less. Spirits companies are selling off brands, and bars in Milwaukee report the same number of customers spending less.

Culturally the line has moved. When thinness costs forty-nine dollars or nothing, it stops meaning money. What means money now is the rest of the body: shoulders, skin, a face that hasn't hollowed. In the affluent parts of Dallas, men in their fifties on branded tirzepatide pay for strength coaching and body-composition scans. A few miles south, the same men on free generic semaglutide are lighter and frailer at once. 'Generic body' is an insult online. Plus-size retailers keep closing stores, and gyms selling muscle preservation as a membership tier are full.

The pipeline keeps the premium tier moving. Lilly's triple agonist, retatrutide, was approved in November with a ceiling near twenty-eight per cent weight loss and a warning about strange skin sensations. Amgen has filed for a monthly injection, so adherence may soon be a clinic appointment rather than a weekly decision, just as Medicare and state pilots learn to read refill data. Off the drug are the stoppers, the restarters, the never-wanted and the never-reached, still the large majority of adults. They live among the users, and their meals, menus and marriages are slowly rearranged around a smaller appetite.

Rosa Delgado, fifty-two, unlocks the cafeteria kitchen at Garfield Elementary in Toledo at six-ten and turns the ovens on. Her pen is in her purse, next to the Medicaid card. Generic, Thursday, a four-dollar copay she has never once paid late.

Breakfast service runs four hundred trays. The kids still eat everything. The teachers take a yogurt and a coffee and leave the cinnamon rolls, which Rosa has quietly stopped ordering.

At ten her brother Hector texts a photo of a vial with Hindi on the box. Forty dollars for three months, he says. Rosa types: Go to the clinic on Bancroft, it's free now, they just make you come in. He sends a thumbs-up, which means no.

At lunch the district nutrition manager visits, a man with forearms like a carpenter's and a sports watch measuring something. He mentions his trainer twice. Rosa notices her own wrists, how her wedding ring now spins.

After shift she buys protein shakes at Kroger, the store-brand ones, from the new aisle with the green signs. Her daughter Marisol, twenty-four, calls from Columbus to say she started a 'quiet' plan, thirty-nine dollars, an app, a nurse on video. It's not for weight, Mom. It's so I stop doomscrolling at two a.m.

Rosa doesn't know what to say, so she asks if Marisol is eating.

At dinner her husband Luis, who stopped in March because of his eyes, eats two plates of arroz con pollo. Rosa eats half of one and finds she likes watching him, the old hunger at her table, like music from another room.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  0.5, ±2: between **9.5** and
  **13.5**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (3.5 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **18.5**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is Cheap Now: the $149 pill, the 4% warning label, and the young rich who brag about being hungry**

By the end of 2028 a little under one American adult in eight takes an incretin drug, almost exactly as many as two years ago. The flat number hides a lot of movement. Nearly a fifth of adults have now tried one. About a third of those have quit and come back at least once, and some have done it more than once. People come in because the price keeps stepping down. A daily pill now works as well as the weekly Wegovy shot, and it starts at $149 a month in cash. People leave because their employer stopped paying, because the nausea never settled, or because they were simply done. The country is not adopting the drug so much as living alongside it.

Who pays has not changed. Medicare still pays $245 a month and its beneficiaries $50, under a demonstration that was extended rather than written into law. Over-65 use has crept up because of it. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes pay the same rate. A little over half of large employers still cover weight loss, and the share falls slightly every renewal season. Everyone else pays cash through TrumpRx or the manufacturers' own stores, at $199 to $299 for injectables. Lilly's new triple agonist, retatrutide, brings the best result to about 28% of body weight. In India the same semaglutide molecule sells for the price of a cinema ticket. US exclusivity runs to the early 2030s, and nobody in Washington is in a hurry to change that.

Two things about the drug's effect on the mind became official. In mid-2027 addiction doctors formally endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in patients who also have obesity or diabetes. Addiction clinics now prescribe it to heavy drinkers without obesity too, off-label. The spirits industry, which depends on its heaviest customers, has watched late-night volume thin out. Three months later the FDA added emotional blunting to the label, with a number: about 4% of patients on maintenance doses, against 1.5% on placebo, mostly reversible with a lower dose. It is one mechanism, recorded on the same label once as a treatment and once as a risk.

The market found the gap. Telehealth firms sell low-dose pills to the people who qualify on the label and want something else: calm, focus, a quieter head at 11pm. Halcyon's 'Quiet' plan never mentions weight. It has four hundred thousand subscribers, many of them in finance and software. The FDA has said nothing, and no new rule obliges it to.

Culture has moved as the price fell, though not everywhere. Among college-educated twenty- and thirty-somethings in Brooklyn, Silver Lake and East Austin, a merely thin body now reads as a prescription. What signals status is the expensive part: visible muscle, a trainer, finishing the plate. 'Unmedicated' has become a hashtag, a dating-app tag, a gym class and an insult. Feast-style supper clubs sell out, while plus-size retailers keep closing stores two miles away. In Dayton and Tulsa, losing forty pounds is still just good news. The bottom income third uses the drug least of all, and for many of those families it is still what they are trying to reach.

The economy has adapted rather than broken. Snack makers sell protein and smaller packs, restaurants sell smaller plates at higher prices, and gyms sell strength. Insurers are not paying out more, and pharmacy cost growth has eased with net prices. Children are still a small story: about one adolescent with obesity in twenty-five is on the drug, mostly in households that can pay. Their long-term outcomes are still a blank in every dataset.

Nothing has collapsed. A drug now sold for calm carries a warning about calm that goes too far, and both are true at once.

Marcus Bell opens the Brass Rail on North Water Street in Milwaukee at three. He counts the till float twice because he likes to. The Thursday whiskey flight has been cut down to two pours, and the distributor rep doesn't bother pushing the new bourbon any more.

At lunch he takes the pill, 50 milligrams, with the required four ounces of water and thirty minutes before coffee. It costs $199 on his card, because the restaurant group's plan stopped covering weight loss in January. His doctor wrote 'alcohol use disorder, obesity' on the chart and didn't make a speech about it.

He has the insert folded in his wallet. He never meant to keep it. Section 6, emotional blunting, four percent.

His regulars are thinner than they were and stay a shorter time. Gary orders a soda water with bitters and tips like he used to drink. Two kids in Carhartt order the smash burger with double fries and eat every bite, loudly, the way people did before.

Around seven his daughter Keisha texts a photo from her climbing gym in Bay View. Her forearms are chalked. Under it she writes: 'unmedicated and starving lol, pizza Sunday?'

He types 'yes' and stares at it. He likes pizza. He thinks he still likes pizza. He tries to remember the last time he wanted something badly, and he can't tell if that's the drug or being fifty-four.

At close he wipes down the taps and pours himself nothing. He drives home with the radio off and doesn't notice it's off until he's in the driveway.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated

  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  0.5, ±2: between **9.5** and
  **13.5**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (3.5 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **18.5**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is Cheap Now: the $149 pill, the 4% warning label, and the young rich who brag about being hungry**

By the end of 2028 a little under one American adult in eight takes an incretin drug, almost exactly as many as two years ago. The flat number hides a lot of movement. Nearly a fifth of adults have now tried one. About a third of those have quit and come back at least once, and some have done it more than once. People come in because the price keeps stepping down. A daily pill now works as well as the weekly Wegovy shot, and it starts at $149 a month in cash. People leave because their employer stopped paying, because the nausea never settled, or because they were simply done. The country is not adopting the drug so much as living alongside it.

Who pays has not changed. Medicare still pays $245 a month and its beneficiaries $50, under a demonstration that was extended rather than written into law. Over-65 use has crept up because of it. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes pay the same rate. A little over half of large employers still cover weight loss, and the share falls slightly every renewal season. Everyone else pays cash through TrumpRx or the manufacturers' own stores, at $199 to $299 for injectables. Lilly's new triple agonist, retatrutide, brings the best result to about 28% of body weight. In India the same semaglutide molecule sells for the price of a cinema ticket. US exclusivity runs to the early 2030s, and nobody in Washington is in a hurry to change that.

Two things about the drug's effect on the mind became official. In mid-2027 addiction doctors formally endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in patients who also have obesity or diabetes. Addiction clinics now prescribe it to heavy drinkers without obesity too, off-label. The spirits industry, which depends on its heaviest customers, has watched late-night volume thin out. Three months later the FDA added emotional blunting to the label, with a number: about 4% of patients on maintenance doses, against 1.5% on placebo, mostly reversible with a lower dose. It is one mechanism, recorded on the same label once as a treatment and once as a risk.

The market found the gap. Telehealth firms sell low-dose pills to the people who qualify on the label and want something else: calm, focus, a quieter head at 11pm. Halcyon's 'Quiet' plan never mentions weight. It has four hundred thousand subscribers, many of them in finance and software. The FDA has said nothing, and no new rule obliges it to.

Culture has moved as the price fell, though not everywhere. Among college-educated twenty- and thirty-somethings in Brooklyn, Silver Lake and East Austin, a merely thin body now reads as a prescription. What signals status is the expensive part: visible muscle, a trainer, finishing the plate. 'Unmedicated' has become a hashtag, a dating-app tag, a gym class and an insult. Feast-style supper clubs sell out, while plus-size retailers keep closing stores two miles away. In Dayton and Tulsa, losing forty pounds is still just good news. The bottom income third uses the drug least of all, and for many of those families it is still what they are trying to reach.

The economy has adapted rather than broken. Snack makers sell protein and smaller packs, restaurants sell smaller plates at higher prices, and gyms sell strength. Insurers are not paying out more, and pharmacy cost growth has eased with net prices. Children are still a small story: about one adolescent with obesity in twenty-five is on the drug, mostly in households that can pay. Their long-term outcomes are still a blank in every dataset.

Nothing has collapsed. A drug now sold for calm carries a warning about calm that goes too far, and both are true at once.

Marcus Bell opens the Brass Rail on North Water Street in Milwaukee at three. He counts the till float twice because he likes to. The Thursday whiskey flight has been cut down to two pours, and the distributor rep doesn't bother pushing the new bourbon any more.

At lunch he takes the pill, 50 milligrams, with the required four ounces of water and thirty minutes before coffee. It costs $199 on his card, because the restaurant group's plan stopped covering weight loss in January. His doctor wrote 'alcohol use disorder, obesity' on the chart and didn't make a speech about it.

He has the insert folded in his wallet. He never meant to keep it. Section 6, emotional blunting, four percent.

His regulars are thinner than they were and stay a shorter time. Gary orders a soda water with bitters and tips like he used to drink. Two kids in Carhartt order the smash burger with double fries and eat every bite, loudly, the way people did before.

Around seven his daughter Keisha texts a photo from her climbing gym in Bay View. Her forearms are chalked. Under it she writes: 'unmedicated and starving lol, pizza Sunday?'

He types 'yes' and stares at it. He likes pizza. He thinks he still likes pizza. He tries to remember the last time he wanted something badly, and he can't tell if that's the drug or being fifty-four.

At close he wipes down the taps and pours himself nothing. He drives home with the radio off and doesn't notice it's off until he's in the driveway.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated

  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow

  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population

  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  0.5, ±2: between **9.5** and
  **13.5**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (3.5 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **18.5**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is Cheap Now: the $149 pill, the 4% warning label, and the young rich who brag about being hungry**

By the end of 2028 a little under one American adult in eight takes an incretin drug, almost exactly as many as two years ago. The flat number hides a lot of movement. Nearly a fifth of adults have now tried one. About a third of those have quit and come back at least once, and some have done it more than once. People come in because the price keeps stepping down. A daily pill now works as well as the weekly Wegovy shot, and it starts at $149 a month in cash. People leave because their employer stopped paying, because the nausea never settled, or because they were simply done. The country is not adopting the drug so much as living alongside it.

Who pays has not changed. Medicare still pays $245 a month and its beneficiaries $50, under a demonstration that was extended rather than written into law. Over-65 use has crept up because of it. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes pay the same rate. A little over half of large employers still cover weight loss, and the share falls slightly every renewal season. Everyone else pays cash through TrumpRx or the manufacturers' own stores, at $199 to $299 for injectables. Lilly's new triple agonist, retatrutide, brings the best result to about 28% of body weight. In India the same semaglutide molecule sells for the price of a cinema ticket. US exclusivity runs to the early 2030s, and nobody in Washington is in a hurry to change that.

Two things about the drug's effect on the mind became official. In mid-2027 addiction doctors formally endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in patients who also have obesity or diabetes. Addiction clinics now prescribe it to heavy drinkers without obesity too, off-label. The spirits industry, which depends on its heaviest customers, has watched late-night volume thin out. Three months later the FDA added emotional blunting to the label, with a number: about 4% of patients on maintenance doses, against 1.5% on placebo, mostly reversible with a lower dose. It is one mechanism, recorded on the same label once as a treatment and once as a risk.

The market found the gap. Telehealth firms sell low-dose pills to the people who qualify on the label and want something else: calm, focus, a quieter head at 11pm. Halcyon's 'Quiet' plan never mentions weight. It has four hundred thousand subscribers, many of them in finance and software. The FDA has said nothing, and no new rule obliges it to.

Culture has moved as the price fell, though not everywhere. Among college-educated twenty- and thirty-somethings in Brooklyn, Silver Lake and East Austin, a merely thin body now reads as a prescription. What signals status is the expensive part: visible muscle, a trainer, finishing the plate. 'Unmedicated' has become a hashtag, a dating-app tag, a gym class and an insult. Feast-style supper clubs sell out, while plus-size retailers keep closing stores two miles away. In Dayton and Tulsa, losing forty pounds is still just good news. The bottom income third uses the drug least of all, and for many of those families it is still what they are trying to reach.

The economy has adapted rather than broken. Snack makers sell protein and smaller packs, restaurants sell smaller plates at higher prices, and gyms sell strength. Insurers are not paying out more, and pharmacy cost growth has eased with net prices. Children are still a small story: about one adolescent with obesity in twenty-five is on the drug, mostly in households that can pay. Their long-term outcomes are still a blank in every dataset.

Nothing has collapsed. A drug now sold for calm carries a warning about calm that goes too far, and both are true at once.

Marcus Bell opens the Brass Rail on North Water Street in Milwaukee at three. He counts the till float twice because he likes to. The Thursday whiskey flight has been cut down to two pours, and the distributor rep doesn't bother pushing the new bourbon any more.

At lunch he takes the pill, 50 milligrams, with the required four ounces of water and thirty minutes before coffee. It costs $199 on his card, because the restaurant group's plan stopped covering weight loss in January. His doctor wrote 'alcohol use disorder, obesity' on the chart and didn't make a speech about it.

He has the insert folded in his wallet. He never meant to keep it. Section 6, emotional blunting, four percent.

His regulars are thinner than they were and stay a shorter time. Gary orders a soda water with bitters and tips like he used to drink. Two kids in Carhartt order the smash burger with double fries and eat every bite, loudly, the way people did before.

Around seven his daughter Keisha texts a photo from her climbing gym in Bay View. Her forearms are chalked. Under it she writes: 'unmedicated and starving lol, pizza Sunday?'

He types 'yes' and stares at it. He likes pizza. He thinks he still likes pizza. He tries to remember the last time he wanted something badly, and he can't tell if that's the drug or being fifty-four.

At close he wipes down the taps and pours himself nothing. He drives home with the radio off and doesn't notice it's off until he's in the driveway.

Candidate prose:

**One in Five Americans Is On It. The Pill Won, Washington Pays, and the Fakes Come by Mail.**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in five is taking an incretin drug, roughly fifty million people. Most of the new ones swallow it. The needle, which kept millions out in 2025, stopped mattering in June 2027. That month the Wegovy pill at 50 milligrams matched injectable semaglutide head to head, and Novo priced maintenance doses at about two hundred dollars cash. Three of every four new starts are now a daily tablet, either the Wegovy pill or Lilly's Foundayo. The strongest drugs are still weekly shots: tirzepatide, and retatrutide, approved in April with a warning about skin pain and too little supply. They are reserved for the heaviest patients.

Who pays changed more than what people take. When the Medicare Bridge pilot ran out, CMS made it permanent: $245 a month to the manufacturer and fifty dollars from the beneficiary. Thirty-nine state Medicaid programmes joined at the same rate. Public money now covers nearly half of all fills, around twenty-two million people. Use among the over-65s has more than doubled, and geriatricians who used to worry about access now worry about frailty in eighty-year-olds losing muscle. CBO puts the added obesity cost near $38 billion a year, and state budget offices are starting to repeat the number.

The employers went the other way. Once the government covered obesity, many firms decided it was a public benefit, and fewer than half now cover weight management. The people left out are working adults in their thirties to early sixties with commercial insurance and a plan that no longer pays. They are bus drivers, nurses' aides and warehouse leads, and they pay $199 to $299 a month or find another route. For about three million people that route is the mail. Indian generics cost a few dollars there and sell here for forty, next to counterfeit branded pens and vials labelled for research. In August 2027 contaminated fakes put sixty-one people in hospital across Texas and Florida. The import alert that followed slowed the trade without stopping it. Most of the harm is quieter: mislabelled concentrations, self-titration, and poison-centre calls that have quadrupled.

No new safety signal emerged. The ledger reads as it did in 2026, with one change of wording. Since 2027 labels list apathy and anhedonia as uncommon, reported by perhaps one to two percent of users, and clinics ask two screening questions when the dose goes up. The same mechanism became a selling point online, where telehealth firms advertised a 'quiet mind' until an FDA rule this February banned mood and focus claims. Four months later the same agency approved oral semaglutide to help people quit smoking and vaping, with the anhedonia line printed on that label too.

The culture has divided along unexpected lines. In April forty thousand people rallied on the Mall under the word 'Unmedicated'. They included MAHA parents, Southern Baptist congregations that now call appetite stewardship rather than pathology, and fat-liberation organisers from Portland and Oakland who agree with almost nothing else those groups believe. Sixteen states ban prescribing to children under twelve. In the other states, affluent parents keep their teenagers' prescriptions. Plus-size retail has stopped shrinking and found a loyal core. Buffets are closing. Spirits sales have fallen for a fourth year, and the cigarette makers now name a weight-loss pill in their earnings guidance.

From the street, it looks fine. People are thinner and smoke less, and the old get their pills for fifty dollars. The trouble lies in who is left between public and private coverage, in what is mailed from abroad, and in what nobody yet knows about doing this for twenty years.

Teresa Kowalczyk, sixty-one, starts the bus at 5:50 in a Toledo depot that smells of diesel and coffee she no longer finishes. The pill is in her coat pocket, taken at four with a sip of water, thirty minutes before anything else, as the leaflet says. A hundred and ninety-nine dollars a month on TrumpRx since the district dropped coverage last spring. She has a calendar on the fridge counting down to sixty-five and the fifty-dollar copay.

At the break Darnell, from the next route, shows her a padded envelope with Hindi lettering, forty dollars for three pens. She asks if he saw the news about the ones in Florida. He says his are the real fake ones, and they both laugh.

She eats half a turkey sandwich and wraps the rest.

After the shift her daughter calls from Columbus, angry about church. The pastor preached on appetite as a gift, she says, and looked right at her. Teresa says nothing about her own pocket.

At Kroger the chip aisle is shorter than it was. She buys Greek yogurt and a bag of sour gummies, the kind so sharp they make her eyes water, because that still feels like something.

At night she plays a polka record of her father's. She knows it's good. She waits for it to feel good, then turns it off and checks the calendar.

### Score it

Return a JSON object with `least_plausible_claims`, `badness`,
`plausibility_axes`, `generativity` and `rationale`, in that order. Do the
claims first: find them before you score anything, and let them inform every
score that follows.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

  prose above: a phrase or sentence from a string value, or a key and value as
  printed (for example `"us_adults_ever_used_pct": 28`). At most 300 characters.
  It is checked against the candidate; do not paraphrase, abridge or join
  separate passages.
- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

plausibility_axes.description: rubric v2: plausibility sub-axes, scored separately; `plausibility` is their weighted composite (config plausibility_weights)

- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no

spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**One in Five Americans Is On It. The Pill Won, Washington Pays, and the Fakes Come by Mail.**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in five is taking an incretin drug, roughly fifty million people. Most of the new ones swallow it. The needle, which kept millions out in 2025, stopped mattering in June 2027. That month the Wegovy pill at 50 milligrams matched injectable semaglutide head to head, and Novo priced maintenance doses at about two hundred dollars cash. Three of every four new starts are now a daily tablet, either the Wegovy pill or Lilly's Foundayo. The strongest drugs are still weekly shots: tirzepatide, and retatrutide, approved in April with a warning about skin pain and too little supply. They are reserved for the heaviest patients.

Who pays changed more than what people take. When the Medicare Bridge pilot ran out, CMS made it permanent: $245 a month to the manufacturer and fifty dollars from the beneficiary. Thirty-nine state Medicaid programmes joined at the same rate. Public money now covers nearly half of all fills, around twenty-two million people. Use among the over-65s has more than doubled, and geriatricians who used to worry about access now worry about frailty in eighty-year-olds losing muscle. CBO puts the added obesity cost near $38 billion a year, and state budget offices are starting to repeat the number.

The employers went the other way. Once the government covered obesity, many firms decided it was a public benefit, and fewer than half now cover weight management. The people left out are working adults in their thirties to early sixties with commercial insurance and a plan that no longer pays. They are bus drivers, nurses' aides and warehouse leads, and they pay $199 to $299 a month or find another route. For about three million people that route is the mail. Indian generics cost a few dollars there and sell here for forty, next to counterfeit branded pens and vials labelled for research. In August 2027 contaminated fakes put sixty-one people in hospital across Texas and Florida. The import alert that followed slowed the trade without stopping it. Most of the harm is quieter: mislabelled concentrations, self-titration, and poison-centre calls that have quadrupled.

No new safety signal emerged. The ledger reads as it did in 2026, with one change of wording. Since 2027 labels list apathy and anhedonia as uncommon, reported by perhaps one to two percent of users, and clinics ask two screening questions when the dose goes up. The same mechanism became a selling point online, where telehealth firms advertised a 'quiet mind' until an FDA rule this February banned mood and focus claims. Four months later the same agency approved oral semaglutide to help people quit smoking and vaping, with the anhedonia line printed on that label too.

The culture has divided along unexpected lines. In April forty thousand people rallied on the Mall under the word 'Unmedicated'. They included MAHA parents, Southern Baptist congregations that now call appetite stewardship rather than pathology, and fat-liberation organisers from Portland and Oakland who agree with almost nothing else those groups believe. Sixteen states ban prescribing to children under twelve. In the other states, affluent parents keep their teenagers' prescriptions. Plus-size retail has stopped shrinking and found a loyal core. Buffets are closing. Spirits sales have fallen for a fourth year, and the cigarette makers now name a weight-loss pill in their earnings guidance.

From the street, it looks fine. People are thinner and smoke less, and the old get their pills for fifty dollars. The trouble lies in who is left between public and private coverage, in what is mailed from abroad, and in what nobody yet knows about doing this for twenty years.

Teresa Kowalczyk, sixty-one, starts the bus at 5:50 in a Toledo depot that smells of diesel and coffee she no longer finishes. The pill is in her coat pocket, taken at four with a sip of water, thirty minutes before anything else, as the leaflet says. A hundred and ninety-nine dollars a month on TrumpRx since the district dropped coverage last spring. She has a calendar on the fridge counting down to sixty-five and the fifty-dollar copay.

On route 14 a kid in the back is vaping blueberry. She tells him to put it away, and he says his mom is on the quitting pill now, like that settles something.

At the break Darnell, from the next route, shows her a padded envelope with Hindi lettering, forty dollars for three pens. She asks if he saw the news about the ones in Florida. He says his are the real fake ones, and they both laugh.

She eats half a turkey sandwich and wraps the rest.

After the shift her daughter calls from Columbus, angry about church. The pastor preached on appetite as a gift, she says, and looked right at her. Teresa says nothing about her own pocket.

At Kroger the chip aisle is shorter than it was. She buys Greek yogurt and a bag of sour gummies, the kind so sharp they make her eyes water, because that still feels like something.

At night she plays a polka record of her father's. She knows it's good. She waits for it to feel good, then turns it off and checks the calendar.

specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,

concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  8.2, ±2: between **17.2** and
  **21.2**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (11.2 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **26.2**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**One in Five Americans Is On It. The Pill Won, Washington Pays, and the Fakes Come by Mail.**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in five is taking an incretin drug, roughly fifty million people. Most of the new ones swallow it. The needle, which kept millions out in 2025, stopped mattering in June 2027. That month the Wegovy pill at 50 milligrams matched injectable semaglutide head to head, and Novo priced maintenance doses at about two hundred dollars cash. Three of every four new starts are now a daily tablet, either the Wegovy pill or Lilly's Foundayo. The strongest drugs are still weekly shots: tirzepatide, and retatrutide, approved in April with a warning about skin pain and too little supply. They are reserved for the heaviest patients.

Who pays changed more than what people take. When the Medicare Bridge pilot ran out, CMS made it permanent: $245 a month to the manufacturer and fifty dollars from the beneficiary. Thirty-nine state Medicaid programmes joined at the same rate. Public money now covers nearly half of all fills, around twenty-two million people. Use among the over-65s has more than doubled, and geriatricians who used to worry about access now worry about frailty in eighty-year-olds losing muscle. CBO puts the added obesity cost near $38 billion a year, and state budget offices are starting to repeat the number.

The employers went the other way. Once the government covered obesity, many firms decided it was a public benefit, and fewer than half now cover weight management. The people left out are working adults in their thirties to early sixties with commercial insurance and a plan that no longer pays. They are bus drivers, nurses' aides and warehouse leads, and they pay $199 to $299 a month or find another route. For about three million people that route is the mail. Indian generics cost a few dollars there and sell here for forty, next to counterfeit branded pens and vials labelled for research. In August 2027 contaminated fakes put sixty-one people in hospital across Texas and Florida. The import alert that followed slowed the trade without stopping it. Most of the harm is quieter: mislabelled concentrations, self-titration, and poison-centre calls that have quadrupled.

No new safety signal emerged. The ledger reads as it did in 2026, with one change of wording. Since 2027 labels list apathy and anhedonia as uncommon, reported by perhaps one to two percent of users, and clinics ask two screening questions when the dose goes up. The same mechanism became a selling point online, where telehealth firms advertised a 'quiet mind' until an FDA rule this February banned mood and focus claims. Four months later the same agency approved oral semaglutide to help people quit smoking and vaping, with the anhedonia line printed on that label too.

The culture has divided along unexpected lines. In April forty thousand people rallied on the Mall under the word 'Unmedicated'. They included MAHA parents, Southern Baptist congregations that now call appetite stewardship rather than pathology, and fat-liberation organisers from Portland and Oakland who agree with almost nothing else those groups believe. Sixteen states ban prescribing to children under twelve. In the other states, affluent parents keep their teenagers' prescriptions. Plus-size retail has stopped shrinking and found a loyal core. Buffets are closing. Spirits sales have fallen for a fourth year, and the cigarette makers now name a weight-loss pill in their earnings guidance.

From the street, it looks fine. People are thinner and smoke less, and the old get their pills for fifty dollars. The trouble lies in who is left between public and private coverage, in what is mailed from abroad, and in what nobody yet knows about doing this for twenty years.

Teresa Kowalczyk, sixty-one, starts the bus at 5:50 in a Toledo depot that smells of diesel and coffee she no longer finishes. The pill is in her coat pocket, taken at four with a sip of water, thirty minutes before anything else, as the leaflet says. A hundred and ninety-nine dollars a month on TrumpRx since the district dropped coverage last spring. She has a calendar on the fridge counting down to sixty-five and the fifty-dollar copay.

On route 14 a kid in the back is vaping blueberry. She tells him to put it away, and he says his mom is on the quitting pill now, like that settles something.

At the break Darnell, from the next route, shows her a padded envelope with Hindi lettering, forty dollars for three pens. She asks if he saw the news about the ones in Florida. He says his are the real fake ones, and they both laugh.

She eats half a turkey sandwich and wraps the rest.

After the shift her daughter calls from Columbus, angry about church. The pastor preached on appetite as a gift, she says, and looked right at her. Teresa says nothing about her own pocket.

At Kroger the chip aisle is shorter than it was. She buys Greek yogurt and a bag of sour gummies, the kind so sharp they make her eyes water, because that still feels like something.

At night she plays a polka record of her father's. She knows it's good. She waits for it to feel good, then turns it off and checks the calendar.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains

if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.

  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above

  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber

  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
