### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  12.2, ±2: between **21.2** and
  **25.2**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (15.2 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **30.2**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**One in Four Americans Is On It, and Their Bodies Show What They Earn**

By the end of 2028 nearly a quarter of American adults say they are taking an incretin drug, and most of the newcomers swallowed rather than injected. Doctors had long said the needle held people back. What actually removed it was a dose: a 50-milligram Wegovy pill that did as well as the weekly injection in a head-to-head trial, plus Lilly's Foundayo, a weaker pill that costs $149 a month at any dose on the TrumpRx portal. Weekly injectables still sit at the top end. Zepbound, CagriSema and, since August, retatrutide with its 28 percent average loss are for the very heavy and the well covered. The ordinary starter now takes a tablet.

Prices fell the way the government's deals said they would. They did not fall the way they fell abroad. In Delhi semaglutide costs less than a sandwich. In Ohio the cheapest branded pill costs $1,788 a year, the injections up to $299 a month, and the old list prices survive only as a reference point. No American generic is coming before the early 2030s. Canada made sure its own was not an option: after border pharmacies in Windsor were emptied in 2027, Ottawa restricted bulk exports.

Employers kept leaving. Fewer than half of large companies now pay for weight loss as such, and those that pay for anything pay for diagnoses: diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea, and since May a dementia-risk label for semaglutide in people over fifty with diabetes. That label is narrow and contested. It came three years after the Alzheimer's trials failed, and neurologists say so on cable news. Still, it changed what the drug means to a 58-year-old with a prediabetic A1c and a father who no longer recognises her. Medicare's obesity coverage outlived the pilot and moved into the planned Part D model at the same $245 rate and $50 copay. It costs roughly twice what the Congressional Budget Office pencilled in, and no one has voted on the difference.

The drugs are also tied up in trade policy now. Tariffs on imported branded medicines spared companies that build in America, so Lilly's Indianapolis-and-Virginia pill gets talked about like a national asset. Novo, which holds the better pill, paid for its exemption with plants and price cuts. Compounders lost their Chinese peptide supply and most of their customers.

What the street sees is class. In Frisco the strength studios have waiting lists, and a lean, visibly muscled body works as a credential, like good teeth. Being merely thin means you are on it. Being heavy increasingly means you work shifts, live out past the county line, or have done the arithmetic and chosen rent. Use runs about twice as high in the top income third as in the bottom. Snack makers are selling brands they built in the 1980s. Discount grocers in Kaufman County have noticed nothing.

The flatness is now a common, ordinary complaint. About a quarter of users say pleasure arrives muted. The standard fix is to take less, or to skip a day or two. Foundayo's short half-life makes the skip work, so Friday has become a pharmacological event. Bartenders know it, musicians time their tours to it, and couples plan anniversaries around it. In addiction clinics the same blunting is the treatment. Nobody has settled whether it is a bug or a feature. People have decided it is a setting.

A third of everyone who has ever started has stopped and come back at least once. Four hundred and forty thousand children are on these drugs, most of them in households that can afford the strength coach too. The trials run about six years. The children may take the drug for sixty.

Denise Ocampo, 44, takes her Foundayo at 6:10 with black coffee standing at the counter in Mesquite. She doesn't take Saturday's, because her niece's quinceañera is Saturday and she wants to taste the tres leches. The orange bottle says $149. The dental group dropped weight coverage last January. The HR email called it 'focusing benefits on clinical conditions.'

At the front desk she checks in Dr. Patel's 9:00, a woman from Frisco with arms like a rowing coach. She is on the Wegovy pill, through her husband's bank plan, she volunteers, as if Denise asked. The 10:30 is Mr. Lyle from Terrell, who is heavy and out of breath and pays his cleaning in two installments.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and puts the other half in the drawer for tomorrow. The girls in billing are talking about a Netflix comedian's bit about 'the flatness.' Denise laughs because it's funny and because it's true. She hasn't wanted to dance since March.

After work she drives her mother's Rybelsus to Balch Springs. Medicare covers it for her diabetes, and since spring the pharmacist has been calling it 'the memory one.' Her mother asks again whether Denise is eating enough. Denise says yes. Her mother tells her she looks like a lady from television, and doesn't mean it as a compliment.

On the way home a billboard on I-30 shows a pill bottle on a flag: MADE HERE. PRICED FOR YOU. She does the math on $149 against the electric bill. Then she sets an alarm to not take Saturday's.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains

if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber

  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,

concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  12.2, ±2: between **21.2** and
  **25.2**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (15.2 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **30.2**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**One in Four Americans Is On It, and Their Bodies Show What They Earn**

By the end of 2028 nearly a quarter of American adults say they are taking an incretin drug, and most of the newcomers swallowed rather than injected. Doctors had long said the needle held people back. What actually removed it was a dose: a 50-milligram Wegovy pill that did as well as the weekly injection in a head-to-head trial, plus Lilly's Foundayo, a weaker pill that costs $149 a month at any dose on the TrumpRx portal. Weekly injectables still sit at the top end. Zepbound, CagriSema and, since August, retatrutide with its 28 percent average loss are for the very heavy and the well covered. The ordinary starter now takes a tablet.

Prices fell the way the government's deals said they would. They did not fall the way they fell abroad. In Delhi semaglutide costs less than a sandwich. In Ohio the cheapest branded pill costs $1,788 a year, the injections up to $299 a month, and the old list prices survive only as a reference point. No American generic is coming before the early 2030s. Canada made sure its own was not an option: after border pharmacies in Windsor were emptied in 2027, Ottawa restricted bulk exports.

Employers kept leaving. Fewer than half of large companies now pay for weight loss as such, and those that pay for anything pay for diagnoses: diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea, and since May a dementia-risk label for semaglutide in people over fifty with diabetes. That label is narrow and contested. It came three years after the Alzheimer's trials failed, and neurologists say so on cable news. Still, it changed what the drug means to a 58-year-old with a prediabetic A1c and a father who no longer recognises her. Medicare's obesity coverage outlived the pilot and moved into the planned Part D model at the same $245 rate and $50 copay. It costs roughly twice what the Congressional Budget Office pencilled in, and no one has voted on the difference.

The drugs are also tied up in trade policy now. Tariffs on imported branded medicines spared companies that build in America, so Lilly's Indianapolis-and-Virginia pill gets talked about like a national asset. Novo, which holds the better pill, paid for its exemption with plants and price cuts. Compounders lost their Chinese peptide supply and most of their customers.

What the street sees is class. In Frisco the strength studios have waiting lists, and a lean, visibly muscled body works as a credential, like good teeth. Being merely thin means you are on it. Being heavy increasingly means you work shifts, live out past the county line, or have done the arithmetic and chosen rent. Use runs about twice as high in the top income third as in the bottom. Snack makers are selling brands they built in the 1980s. Discount grocers in Kaufman County have noticed nothing.

The flatness is now a common, ordinary complaint. About a quarter of users say pleasure arrives muted. The standard fix is to take less, or to skip a day or two. Foundayo's short half-life makes the skip work, so Friday has become a pharmacological event. Bartenders know it, musicians time their tours to it, and couples plan anniversaries around it. In addiction clinics the same blunting is the treatment. Nobody has settled whether it is a bug or a feature. People have decided it is a setting.

A third of everyone who has ever started has stopped and come back at least once. Four hundred and forty thousand children are on these drugs, most of them in households that can afford the strength coach too. The trials run about six years. The children may take the drug for sixty.

Denise Ocampo, 44, takes her Foundayo at 6:10 with black coffee standing at the counter in Mesquite. She doesn't take Saturday's, because her niece's quinceañera is Saturday and she wants to taste the tres leches. The orange bottle says $149. The dental group dropped weight coverage last January. The HR email called it 'focusing benefits on clinical conditions.'

At the front desk she checks in Dr. Patel's 9:00, a woman from Frisco with arms like a rowing coach. She is on the Wegovy pill, through her husband's bank plan, she volunteers, as if Denise asked. The 10:30 is Mr. Lyle from Terrell, who is heavy and out of breath and pays his cleaning in two installments.

At lunch she eats half a turkey wrap and puts the other half in the drawer for tomorrow. The girls in billing are talking about a Netflix comedian's bit about 'the flatness.' Denise laughs because it's funny and because it's true. She hasn't wanted to dance since March.

After work she drives her mother's Rybelsus to Balch Springs. Medicare covers it for her diabetes, and since spring the pharmacist has been calling it 'the memory one.' Her mother asks again whether Denise is eating enough. Denise says yes. Her mother tells her she looks like a lady from television, and doesn't mean it as a compliment.

On the way home a billboard on I-30 shows a pill bottle on a flag: MADE HERE. PRICED FOR YOU. She does the math on $149 against the electric bill. Then she sets an alarm to not take Saturday's.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this

- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the

  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`

  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share

spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a

**One in six Americans is on it. The pill now sells calm, gambling is a craving, and the unmedicated are throwing dinner parties**

By the end of 2028, about one American adult in six, roughly 43 million people, takes an incretin drug. Another sixteen million have taken one and stopped, most because a benefit changed or a bill came due. A third of those who ever started have stopped and come back at least once. Nobody calls this a crisis. It is how the drug is used: weekly or daily, for years, interrupted by insurance.

The price fell the way it was negotiated to fall. Cash injectables cost $199 to $299 a month through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' own channels, and the pills start at $149. Medicare still pays $245 and the beneficiary $50 through a Bridge programme CMS quietly extended to the end of 2029. It now enrols about 2.4 million people and costs about seven billion dollars a year, well above what the budget office expected. Employers keep drifting away, and only 55 percent now cover weight loss. This explains the class shape: 21 percent of the top income third is on the drug, 11 percent of the bottom. Across the northern border, a generic costs a third of the cheapest American brand.

The Lilly–Novo duopoly is fine. Retatrutide arrived in April with 28 percent weight loss. Lilly's muscle-sparing combination with bimagrumab is not approved, but its trial results and filing were enough for strength gyms and longevity clinics to declare the 'skinny-frail' problem over. The FDA's draft guidance asks for proof that patients can climb stairs, not just DEXA scans, and almost nobody read it.

The bigger change is in what the drug is understood to do. In October oral semaglutide was approved for gambling disorder, the first time a regulator wrote 'urge' onto an incretin label. Telehealth companies had already been selling low-dose plans in the language of wellness: calm, focus, freedom from noise. The largest, Quietly, has a million subscribers. The FDA sends letters about the adjectives. The prescriptions are legal. A 2027 study suggested that about one user in ten experiences a real loss of pleasure, and a larger number feel a quiet they would pay for. Sportsbooks now list incretins as a business risk. Kentucky distillers have cut shifts.

The counter-movement started at dinner. In Philadelphia's Fishtown and South Kensington, 'Hungry' supper clubs serve family-style platters to long tables of people who call themselves unmedicated. Their aesthetic is butter, film photos and sweat, and it has spread to Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Austin. Dating apps added a medication field after campaigns from both sides, and 'unmedicated' is now the fastest-growing self-description among young city users. The movement has no single politics. It includes fat-liberation activists angry at pharma pricing and natural-body conservatives who distrust pharma on principle. It also includes people who could not afford the drug and have made that an identity. In this year's presidential race, candidates were asked on stage whether they take it.

In March a Scandinavian registry and a Veterans Affairs cohort found something no trial was long enough to see. People who stopped after five or more years of continuous use, mostly diabetics who started around 2018, were nearly twice as likely to have gastric dysmotility that persisted for months afterwards. The absolute numbers are small and the FDA issued a communication, not a warning. But the paradigm is lifelong therapy, the cohort past five years grows every month, and the evidence that people can safely stop after long use has just got worse.

From the outside things look calm. Restaurants serve half-portions, children grow up watching one parent eat almost nothing, and the drug is now marketed partly for how little it lets people feel.

Rosa Delgado wakes at 5:40 in Columbus and does her Tuesday shot before coffee, left thigh. Ozempic, eight years now, $25 copay through the dental group's plan, because it's for her diabetes and nobody argues about diabetes. She drinks half the coffee.

At work, between cleanings, Tanya from the front desk shows her the Quietly app. Forty-nine dollars the first month on the $149 pill, then $199. Tanya isn't heavy. She says it's for the scrolling, the 2 a.m. carts. "I just don't want things as much. It's nice." Rosa says that sounds nice and means something else.

Lunch is a yogurt she finishes at three.

In the parking lot she rereads the article her sister sent: five years, stomach, after stopping. She has passed five years already. She books the gastroenterologist the app offers for February, then cancels it, then books it again.

Her husband Luis is watching the Browns with the sound off and no betting app open, which she notices. He went on the Wegovy pill in the spring when his job still covered it. He says he just doesn't care who wins anymore. He says it like good news.

At seven their daughter Marisol, twenty-two, comes for dinner. She's bringing the crowd from her Hungry table. Six of them fill the kitchen with garlic and a pan of rice the size of a tire, and they laugh too loud. One boy has a T-shirt that says I FEEL ALL OF IT.

Rosa makes herself a plate, small. She watches her daughter eat seconds, then thirds, and feels something she can't name. It might be envy, or something like grief.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated

  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population

  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.

**One in six Americans is on it. The pill now sells calm, gambling is a craving, and the unmedicated are throwing dinner parties**

By the end of 2028, about one American adult in six, roughly 43 million people, takes an incretin drug. Another sixteen million have taken one and stopped, most because a benefit changed or a bill came due. A third of those who ever started have stopped and come back at least once. Nobody calls this a crisis. It is how the drug is used: weekly or daily, for years, interrupted by insurance.

The price fell the way it was negotiated to fall. Cash injectables cost $199 to $299 a month through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' own channels, and the pills start at $149. Medicare still pays $245 and the beneficiary $50 through a Bridge programme CMS quietly extended to the end of 2029. It now enrols about 2.4 million people and costs about seven billion dollars a year, well above what the budget office expected. Employers keep drifting away, and only 55 percent now cover weight loss. This explains the class shape: 21 percent of the top income third is on the drug, 11 percent of the bottom. Across the northern border, a generic costs a third of the cheapest American brand.

The Lilly–Novo duopoly is fine. Retatrutide arrived in April with 28 percent weight loss. Lilly's muscle-sparing combination with bimagrumab is not approved, but its trial results and filing were enough for strength gyms and longevity clinics to declare the 'skinny-frail' problem over. The FDA's draft guidance asks for proof that patients can climb stairs, not just DEXA scans, and almost nobody read it.

The bigger change is in what the drug is understood to do. In October oral semaglutide was approved for gambling disorder, the first time a regulator wrote 'urge' onto an incretin label. Telehealth companies had already been selling low-dose plans in the language of wellness: calm, focus, freedom from noise. The largest, Quietly, has a million subscribers. The FDA sends letters about the adjectives. The prescriptions are legal. A 2027 study suggested that about one user in ten experiences a real loss of pleasure, and a larger number feel a quiet they would pay for. Sportsbooks now list incretins as a business risk. Kentucky distillers have cut shifts.

The counter-movement started at dinner. In Philadelphia's Fishtown and South Kensington, 'Hungry' supper clubs serve family-style platters to long tables of people who call themselves unmedicated. Their aesthetic is butter, film photos and sweat, and it has spread to Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Austin. Dating apps added a medication field after campaigns from both sides, and 'unmedicated' is now the fastest-growing self-description among young city users. The movement has no single politics. It includes fat-liberation activists angry at pharma pricing and natural-body conservatives who distrust pharma on principle. It also includes people who could not afford the drug and have made that an identity. In this year's presidential race, candidates were asked on stage whether they take it.

In March a Scandinavian registry and a Veterans Affairs cohort found something no trial was long enough to see. People who stopped after five or more years of continuous use, mostly diabetics who started around 2018, were nearly twice as likely to have gastric dysmotility that persisted for months afterwards. The absolute numbers are small and the FDA issued a communication, not a warning. But the paradigm is lifelong therapy, the cohort past five years grows every month, and the evidence that people can safely stop after long use has just got worse.

From the outside things look calm. Restaurants serve half-portions, children grow up watching one parent eat almost nothing, and the drug is now marketed partly for how little it lets people feel.

Rosa Delgado wakes at 5:40 in Columbus and does her Tuesday shot before coffee, left thigh. Ozempic, eight years now, $25 copay through the dental group's plan, because it's for her diabetes and nobody argues about diabetes. She drinks half the coffee.

At work, between cleanings, Tanya from the front desk shows her the Quietly app. Forty-nine dollars the first month on the $149 pill, then $199. Tanya isn't heavy. She says it's for the scrolling, the 2 a.m. carts. "I just don't want things as much. It's nice." Rosa says that sounds nice and means something else.

Lunch is a yogurt she finishes at three.

In the parking lot she rereads the article her sister sent: five years, stomach, after stopping. She has passed five years already. She books the gastroenterologist the app offers for February, then cancels it, then books it again.

Her husband Luis is watching the Browns with the sound off and no betting app open, which she notices. He went on the Wegovy pill in the spring when his job still covered it. He says he just doesn't care who wins anymore. He says it like good news.

At seven their daughter Marisol, twenty-two, comes for dinner. She's bringing the crowd from her Hungry table. Six of them fill the kitchen with garlic and a pan of rice the size of a tire, and they laugh too loud. One boy has a T-shirt that says I FEEL ALL OF IT.

Rosa makes herself a plate, small. She watches her daughter eat seconds, then thirds, and feels something she can't name. It might be envy, or something like grief.

Candidate prose:

**One in six Americans is on it. The pill now sells calm, gambling is a craving, and the unmedicated are throwing dinner parties**

By the end of 2028, about one American adult in six, roughly 43 million people, takes an incretin drug. Another sixteen million have taken one and stopped, most because a benefit changed or a bill came due. A third of those who ever started have stopped and come back at least once. Nobody calls this a crisis. It is how the drug is used: weekly or daily, for years, interrupted by insurance.

The price fell the way it was negotiated to fall. Cash injectables cost $199 to $299 a month through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' own channels, and the pills start at $149. Medicare still pays $245 and the beneficiary $50 through a Bridge programme CMS quietly extended to the end of 2029. It now enrols about 2.4 million people and costs about seven billion dollars a year, well above what the budget office expected. Employers keep drifting away, and only 55 percent now cover weight loss. This explains the class shape: 21 percent of the top income third is on the drug, 11 percent of the bottom. Across the northern border, a generic costs a third of the cheapest American brand.

The Lilly–Novo duopoly is fine. Retatrutide arrived in April with 28 percent weight loss. Lilly's muscle-sparing combination with bimagrumab is not approved, but its trial results and filing were enough for strength gyms and longevity clinics to declare the 'skinny-frail' problem over. The FDA's draft guidance asks for proof that patients can climb stairs, not just DEXA scans, and almost nobody read it.

The bigger change is in what the drug is understood to do. In October oral semaglutide was approved for gambling disorder, the first time a regulator wrote 'urge' onto an incretin label. Telehealth companies had already been selling low-dose plans in the language of wellness: calm, focus, freedom from noise. The largest, Quietly, has a million subscribers. The FDA sends letters about the adjectives. The prescriptions are legal. A 2027 study suggested that about one user in ten experiences a real loss of pleasure, and a larger number feel a quiet they would pay for. Sportsbooks now list incretins as a business risk. Kentucky distillers have cut shifts.

The counter-movement started at dinner. In Philadelphia's Fishtown and South Kensington, 'Hungry' supper clubs serve family-style platters to long tables of people who call themselves unmedicated. Their aesthetic is butter, film photos and sweat, and it has spread to Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Austin. Dating apps added a medication field after campaigns from both sides, and 'unmedicated' is now the fastest-growing self-description among young city users. The movement has no single politics. It includes fat-liberation activists angry at pharma pricing and natural-body conservatives who distrust pharma on principle. It also includes people who could not afford the drug and have made that an identity. In this year's presidential race, candidates were asked on stage whether they take it.

In March a Scandinavian registry and a Veterans Affairs cohort found something no trial was long enough to see. People who stopped after five or more years of continuous use, mostly diabetics who started around 2018, were nearly twice as likely to have gastric dysmotility that persisted for months afterwards. The absolute numbers are small and the FDA issued a communication, not a warning. But the paradigm is lifelong therapy, the cohort past five years grows every month, and the evidence that people can safely stop after long use has just got worse.

From the outside things look calm. Restaurants serve half-portions, children grow up watching one parent eat almost nothing, and the drug is now marketed partly for how little it lets people feel.

Rosa Delgado wakes at 5:40 in Columbus and does her Tuesday shot before coffee, left thigh. Ozempic, eight years now, $25 copay through the dental group's plan, because it's for her diabetes and nobody argues about diabetes. She drinks half the coffee.

At work, between cleanings, Tanya from the front desk shows her the Quietly app. Forty-nine dollars the first month on the $149 pill, then $199. Tanya isn't heavy. She says it's for the scrolling, the 2 a.m. carts. "I just don't want things as much. It's nice." Rosa says that sounds nice and means something else.

Lunch is a yogurt she finishes at three.

In the parking lot she rereads the article her sister sent: five years, stomach, after stopping. She has passed five years already. She books the gastroenterologist the app offers for February, then cancels it, then books it again.

Her husband Luis is watching the Browns with the sound off and no betting app open, which she notices. He went on the Wegovy pill in the spring when his job still covered it. He says he just doesn't care who wins anymore. He says it like good news.

At seven their daughter Marisol, twenty-two, comes for dinner. She's bringing the crowd from her Hungry table. Six of them fill the kitchen with garlic and a pan of rice the size of a tire, and they laugh too loud. One boy has a T-shirt that says I FEEL ALL OF IT.

Rosa makes herself a plate, small. She watches her daughter eat seconds, then thirds, and feels something she can't name. It might be envy, or something like grief.

- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

**One in Four: Generic Ozempic costs $49, your boss tracks your refills, and the new worry is your grandmother's hip**

By the end of 2028 a quarter of American adults take an incretin drug, and almost nobody remarks on it. What people remark on is not being on one. A pregnant woman, a man with gastroparesis, a twenty-four-year-old who lifts and calls himself 'natty', a colleague who has chosen to pay the wellness surcharge: these are the people who get asked.

Price did most of this. In June 2027 Novo Nordisk settled its semaglutide patent fight with Viatris and Teva, and in January 2028 authorised generic injectable semaglutide reached pharmacies at $49 to $69 a month. Wegovy's list price still says $1,349, a number that now exists mainly in court filings. Tirzepatide stays branded and dearer, Lilly's oral Foundayo still starts at $149 on TrumpRx, and retatrutide, the triple agonist approved in April, takes off another quarter of body weight for people sick enough to qualify. Compounding pharmacies are gone; the gray market has dwindled to online 'research peptide' vendors.

Cheap did not mean unconditional. When the Medicare Bridge pilot expired, CMS replaced it with an outcomes model. Coverage continues only if refills cover 80 percent of days, weight or HbA1c moves within six months, and anyone over 65 has a DEXA scan and squeezes a grip dynamometer once a year. At roughly nine million Medicare users and a blended $131 a month, the programme costs about $14 billion a year. Employers that dropped coverage in 2026 came back because the generic costs a fifth as much, but they came back with terms attached. In March, federal guidance confirmed that wellness programmes could use pharmacy refill data as an adherence standard, and about a third of large employers now charge a premium differential to staff who miss their targets and do not take the 'reasonable alternative'. Eleven state Medicaid programmes attach similar conditions. Access is now limited less by income than by keeping up with the paperwork, which falls hardest on the uninsured poor in non-expansion states and on anyone whose life is too irregular to refill on schedule.

The worry that grew fastest was not appetite but bones. A Medicare cohort published in August 2027 found that older long-term users who lost more than 15 percent of their weight had about 30 percent more hip and vertebral fractures, and the FDA added lean-mass and bone warnings across the class that October. Sarcopenia codes are up by two-fifths among older users. Strength gyms, physical-therapy clinics and pharmacy grip-strength kiosks are the growth businesses. In June Lilly launched 'Zepbound Strong', tirzepatide boxed with a training app and a leucine medical food, advertised as solving the 'skinny-frail' problem. The drug inside is unchanged, and the pharmacological muscle drugs are still in phase three. Affluent users buy the co-pack and a trainer; most others get the generic and a pamphlet.

The flattening that was a curiosity in 2026 is now a routine complaint. A 2027 cohort put clinically meaningful anhedonia at about one user in six, mostly reversible with a lower dose. Obesity-medicine guidance now endorses scheduled 'drug holidays', and families plan them around Thanksgiving, weddings and anniversaries. Insurers tolerate them only within the 80 percent rule, which works out to roughly six missed days a month, and people do that sum in their heads. Sex therapists ask about doses at intake. Bars report busy holiday weekends.

The food industry has adapted rather than collapsed. In Columbus, Ohio, single-serve snack packs outsell family bags, and casual chains offer half plates without being asked. Spirits keep losing their heaviest drinkers, partly to off-label prescriptions the FDA has still not approved. Politically, the drug has unusual opponents. Privacy advocates, fat-acceptance groups and MAHA conservatives all oppose refill surveillance, while the administration that negotiated the prices defends the conditions as the cost of making the drug cheap.

Denise Alvarado wakes at 5:40 in San Antonio and checks the app before the coffee. Adherence: 83 percent. Green. She took the holiday for Marisol's baby shower, and it cost her four points.

The generic pen is in the butter compartment. Tuesday is pen day. She pinches her belly, counts ten, and drops the pen in the coffee can of sharps on top of the fridge.

At the hospital payroll office, Teresa from benefits is walking the floor with a clipboard. Open enrollment. Forty-five dollars a paycheck if you're not in the program or haven't hit target. Teresa says it nicely. Denise is in the program.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. She wraps the other half for later and forgets it.

After work she drives her mother to the Walgreens on Bandera for the grip test. Her mother is eighty-one, on the Medicare generic, ten dollars a month. She squeezes the handle with both hands though the tech says one. Fourteen kilograms. Last year it was seventeen. The tech prints a sheet that says RESISTANCE TRAINING in capitals and recommends a bone scan.

'I lift the laundry,' her mother says.

At home, her son Mateo is eating cereal from a mixing bowl at the counter, a bowl the size of a hubcap. He's twenty-four and has never been on it. He's proud of that, the way her father was proud of never seeing a doctor.

'You want some?' he says.

She watches him eat and feels nothing in particular, which she has learned to notice. Then she takes her mother's sheet and sticks it to the fridge.

  printed (for example `"us_adults_ever_used_pct": 28`). At most 300 characters.
  It is checked against the candidate; do not paraphrase, abridge or join
  separate passages.
- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

plausibility_axes.description: rubric v2: plausibility sub-axes, scored separately; `plausibility` is their weighted composite (config plausibility_weights)

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  14.1, ±2: between **23.1** and
  **27.1**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (17.1 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **32.1**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

The generator was given this same envelope. Score `magnitude` against it.

**One in Four: Generic Ozempic costs $49, your boss tracks your refills, and the new worry is your grandmother's hip**

By the end of 2028 a quarter of American adults take an incretin drug, and almost nobody remarks on it. What people remark on is not being on one. A pregnant woman, a man with gastroparesis, a twenty-four-year-old who lifts and calls himself 'natty', a colleague who has chosen to pay the wellness surcharge: these are the people who get asked.

Price did most of this. In June 2027 Novo Nordisk settled its semaglutide patent fight with Viatris and Teva, and in January 2028 authorised generic injectable semaglutide reached pharmacies at $49 to $69 a month. Wegovy's list price still says $1,349, a number that now exists mainly in court filings. Tirzepatide stays branded and dearer, Lilly's oral Foundayo still starts at $149 on TrumpRx, and retatrutide, the triple agonist approved in April, takes off another quarter of body weight for people sick enough to qualify. Compounding pharmacies are gone; the gray market has dwindled to online 'research peptide' vendors.

Cheap did not mean unconditional. When the Medicare Bridge pilot expired, CMS replaced it with an outcomes model. Coverage continues only if refills cover 80 percent of days, weight or HbA1c moves within six months, and anyone over 65 has a DEXA scan and squeezes a grip dynamometer once a year. At roughly nine million Medicare users and a blended $131 a month, the programme costs about $14 billion a year. Employers that dropped coverage in 2026 came back because the generic costs a fifth as much, but they came back with terms attached. In March, federal guidance confirmed that wellness programmes could use pharmacy refill data as an adherence standard, and about a third of large employers now charge a premium differential to staff who miss their targets and do not take the 'reasonable alternative'. Eleven state Medicaid programmes attach similar conditions. Access is now limited less by income than by keeping up with the paperwork, which falls hardest on the uninsured poor in non-expansion states and on anyone whose life is too irregular to refill on schedule.

The worry that grew fastest was not appetite but bones. A Medicare cohort published in August 2027 found that older long-term users who lost more than 15 percent of their weight had about 30 percent more hip and vertebral fractures, and the FDA added lean-mass and bone warnings across the class that October. Sarcopenia codes are up by two-fifths among older users. Strength gyms, physical-therapy clinics and pharmacy grip-strength kiosks are the growth businesses. In June Lilly launched 'Zepbound Strong', tirzepatide boxed with a training app and a leucine medical food, advertised as solving the 'skinny-frail' problem. The drug inside is unchanged, and the pharmacological muscle drugs are still in phase three. Affluent users buy the co-pack and a trainer; most others get the generic and a pamphlet.

The flattening that was a curiosity in 2026 is now a routine complaint. A 2027 cohort put clinically meaningful anhedonia at about one user in six, mostly reversible with a lower dose. Obesity-medicine guidance now endorses scheduled 'drug holidays', and families plan them around Thanksgiving, weddings and anniversaries. Insurers tolerate them only within the 80 percent rule, which works out to roughly six missed days a month, and people do that sum in their heads. Sex therapists ask about doses at intake. Bars report busy holiday weekends.

The food industry has adapted rather than collapsed. In Columbus, Ohio, single-serve snack packs outsell family bags, and casual chains offer half plates without being asked. Spirits keep losing their heaviest drinkers, partly to off-label prescriptions the FDA has still not approved. Politically, the drug has unusual opponents. Privacy advocates, fat-acceptance groups and MAHA conservatives all oppose refill surveillance, while the administration that negotiated the prices defends the conditions as the cost of making the drug cheap.

Denise Alvarado wakes at 5:40 in San Antonio and checks the app before the coffee. Adherence: 83 percent. Green. She took the holiday for Marisol's baby shower, and it cost her four points.

The generic pen is in the butter compartment. Tuesday is pen day. She pinches her belly, counts ten, and drops the pen in the coffee can of sharps on top of the fridge.

At the hospital payroll office, Teresa from benefits is walking the floor with a clipboard. Open enrollment. Forty-five dollars a paycheck if you're not in the program or haven't hit target. Teresa says it nicely. Denise is in the program.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. She wraps the other half for later and forgets it.

After work she drives her mother to the Walgreens on Bandera for the grip test. Her mother is eighty-one, on the Medicare generic, ten dollars a month. She squeezes the handle with both hands though the tech says one. Fourteen kilograms. Last year it was seventeen. The tech prints a sheet that says RESISTANCE TRAINING in capitals and recommends a bone scan.

'I lift the laundry,' her mother says.

At home, her son Mateo is eating cereal from a mixing bowl at the counter, a bowl the size of a hubcap. He's twenty-four and has never been on it. He's proud of that, the way her father was proud of never seeing a doctor.

'You want some?' he says.

She watches him eat and feels nothing in particular, which she has learned to notice. Then she takes her mother's sheet and sticks it to the fridge.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  14.1, ±2: between **23.1** and
  **27.1**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (17.1 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **32.1**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.

  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**One in Four: Generic Ozempic costs $49, your boss tracks your refills, and the new worry is your grandmother's hip**

By the end of 2028 a quarter of American adults take an incretin drug, and almost nobody remarks on it. What people remark on is not being on one. A pregnant woman, a man with gastroparesis, a twenty-four-year-old who lifts and calls himself 'natty', a colleague who has chosen to pay the wellness surcharge: these are the people who get asked.

Price did most of this. In June 2027 Novo Nordisk settled its semaglutide patent fight with Viatris and Teva, and in January 2028 authorised generic injectable semaglutide reached pharmacies at $49 to $69 a month. Wegovy's list price still says $1,349, a number that now exists mainly in court filings. Tirzepatide stays branded and dearer, Lilly's oral Foundayo still starts at $149 on TrumpRx, and retatrutide, the triple agonist approved in April, takes off another quarter of body weight for people sick enough to qualify. Compounding pharmacies are gone; the gray market has dwindled to online 'research peptide' vendors.

Cheap did not mean unconditional. When the Medicare Bridge pilot expired, CMS replaced it with an outcomes model. Coverage continues only if refills cover 80 percent of days, weight or HbA1c moves within six months, and anyone over 65 has a DEXA scan and squeezes a grip dynamometer once a year. At roughly nine million Medicare users and a blended $131 a month, the programme costs about $14 billion a year. Employers that dropped coverage in 2026 came back because the generic costs a fifth as much, but they came back with terms attached. In March, federal guidance confirmed that wellness programmes could use pharmacy refill data as an adherence standard, and about a third of large employers now charge a premium differential to staff who miss their targets and do not take the 'reasonable alternative'. Eleven state Medicaid programmes attach similar conditions. Access is now limited less by income than by keeping up with the paperwork, which falls hardest on the uninsured poor in non-expansion states and on anyone whose life is too irregular to refill on schedule.

The worry that grew fastest was not appetite but bones. A Medicare cohort published in August 2027 found that older long-term users who lost more than 15 percent of their weight had about 30 percent more hip and vertebral fractures, and the FDA added lean-mass and bone warnings across the class that October. Sarcopenia codes are up by two-fifths among older users. Strength gyms, physical-therapy clinics and pharmacy grip-strength kiosks are the growth businesses. In June Lilly launched 'Zepbound Strong', tirzepatide boxed with a training app and a leucine medical food, advertised as solving the 'skinny-frail' problem. The drug inside is unchanged, and the pharmacological muscle drugs are still in phase three. Affluent users buy the co-pack and a trainer; most others get the generic and a pamphlet.

The flattening that was a curiosity in 2026 is now a routine complaint. A 2027 cohort put clinically meaningful anhedonia at about one user in six, mostly reversible with a lower dose. Obesity-medicine guidance now endorses scheduled 'drug holidays', and families plan them around Thanksgiving, weddings and anniversaries. Insurers tolerate them only within the 80 percent rule, which works out to roughly six missed days a month, and people do that sum in their heads. Sex therapists ask about doses at intake. Bars report busy holiday weekends.

The food industry has adapted rather than collapsed. In Columbus, Ohio, single-serve snack packs outsell family bags, and casual chains offer half plates without being asked. Spirits keep losing their heaviest drinkers, partly to off-label prescriptions the FDA has still not approved. Politically, the drug has unusual opponents. Privacy advocates, fat-acceptance groups and MAHA conservatives all oppose refill surveillance, while the administration that negotiated the prices defends the conditions as the cost of making the drug cheap.

Denise Alvarado wakes at 5:40 in San Antonio and checks the app before the coffee. Adherence: 83 percent. Green. She took the holiday for Marisol's baby shower, and it cost her four points.

The generic pen is in the butter compartment. Tuesday is pen day. She pinches her belly, counts ten, and drops the pen in the coffee can of sharps on top of the fridge.

At the hospital payroll office, Teresa from benefits is walking the floor with a clipboard. Open enrollment. Forty-five dollars a paycheck if you're not in the program or haven't hit target. Teresa says it nicely. Denise is in the program.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. She wraps the other half for later and forgets it.

After work she drives her mother to the Walgreens on Bandera for the grip test. Her mother is eighty-one, on the Medicare generic, ten dollars a month. She squeezes the handle with both hands though the tech says one. Fourteen kilograms. Last year it was seventeen. The tech prints a sheet that says RESISTANCE TRAINING in capitals and recommends a bone scan.

'I lift the laundry,' her mother says.

At home, her son Mateo is eating cereal from a mixing bowl at the counter, a bowl the size of a hubcap. He's twenty-four and has never been on it. He's proud of that, the way her father was proud of never seeing a doctor.

'You want some?' he says.

She watches him eat and feels nothing in particular, which she has learned to notice. Then she takes her mother's sheet and sticks it to the fridge.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  9.4, ±2: between **18.4** and
  **22.4**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (12.4 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **27.4**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is Cheap Now. Muscle Isn't: How a $49 Pill Turned the American Body Into a Pay Stub**

By the end of 2028, one American adult in five takes an incretin drug, about 54 million people. Most of the recent starters never touched a needle. Since Novo Nordisk put out an unbranded version of its own semaglutide in the autumn of 2027, the pill costs $69 a month and the pen $49. That puts the starting price below a phone bill and close to a gym membership. The patents have not expired. Novo chose to undersell itself rather than lose the volume to Lilly, to Indian generics arriving by mail, and to the compounders it spent 2026 suing. The higher-dose Wegovy pill approved in March 2027 does what the injection does, so for most people the needle stopped being a reason not to start.

Who pays has barely changed. Fifty-eight percent of large employers still cover weight-loss drugs, almost the same share as two years earlier, and most now require patients to try the cheap generic before anything stronger. Medicare still pays $245 and still charges beneficiaries $50. That rate carried over when the Bridge pilot ended into the program CMS had already scheduled to follow it. Use among Americans over 65 has nearly doubled. Medicaid coverage depends on which state you live in. The barrier for the bottom income third is no longer the price. It is a prescription, a pharmacy that keeps the product in stock, and the time to deal with both. Use in that group sits at about 14 percent, against 26 percent in the top third.

So the line has moved. In Scottsdale, the people who are thin also have shoulders. They take tirzepatide, or since May the newly approved retatrutide at $499, and they pay a trainer and a clinic that scans their lean mass every quarter. In west Phoenix the thinness came from a pill bottle and looks like it: narrow, soft at the edges, faces a little hollow, the weight returning when a month gets tight. Restaurant managers, apparel buyers and dating apps have all learned to read the difference. The larger bodies that remain are increasingly found among people who could not tolerate the drug or never got a prescription. They are now read as signs of being poor, not of eating too much.

A third of everyone who has ever used the drugs has stopped and started again. Since obesity-medicine societies accepted the practice in late 2027, stopping on purpose has been normal. People take a 'holiday' for Thanksgiving, for a wedding, for an anniversary, to feel hungry or to feel anything much. About one user in five says pleasure is muted at maintenance doses. Couples plan their off-weeks together, and comedians build sets around them. Addiction clinics prescribe the same flatness on purpose to people who drink heavily. No one has measured what years of repeated weight loss and regain do to the body.

The lawyers are not waiting for that research. The federal litigation in Philadelphia has passed twenty-one thousand cases, and the claims have shifted from gastroparesis to pancreatitis and bowel obstruction. The underlying science still shows a small risk, but a small risk across 54 million people produces a lot of plaintiffs. The first jury will be seated in late 2028.

Alongside the pharmacy counter runs a market that has outgrown its regulators. Retatrutide was sold in gyms as a 'research peptide' for a year before the FDA approved it, and it still is, at a fifth of the price. The 2026 rule meant to shut down compounding is still a proposal, and the warning letters arrive at the old rate. Alcohol sales keep falling, snack volumes erode by a few points a year, and plus-size retailers keep closing stores. From the street the country looks healthier. It is also a country where people can read your income from your body.

Denise Ruiz takes the pill at 5:40, with four ounces of water, standing at the sink in the dark. Then thirty minutes without coffee. She uses them to pack her lunch: a shake, a cheese stick, half an apple she probably won't finish.

The bottle says SEMAGLUTIDE TABLETS 25 MG. No brand name, $69 at the Walgreens on Indian School Road. The agency she works for doesn't cover it. She gets her hours and that's it.

Her first client is Mrs. Halvorsen in Arcadia, eighty-one, on the Medicare one. She complains she can't taste her soup. Denise salts it more than she should.

At noon she drives to the second house. The son is home, forty-something, arms like a mover's. A box from somewhere sits open on the counter: little glass vials, a printed label, NOT FOR HUMAN USE. He sees her look and laughs. "Reta," he says. "Everybody at my gym."

In the car she drinks the shake and watches a lawyer on her phone ask whether she or a loved one has had pancreatitis. She hasn't. She swipes it away.

Her sister texts: Saturday is Mateo's graduation party. Carnitas. You going off for it?

Denise looks at herself in the rearview mirror. Her face is thinner than her mother's ever was, and her arms are thinner too. She can't remember the last time she wanted anything badly.

She types: Thursday I'll stop. Then deletes it. Then types it again.

At home her son eats cereal standing up. She sits across from him and isn't hungry. She asks about his day and means it, mostly.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no

  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the

  the driver.
