**Thin Is Cheap Now: the $149 pill, the missing middle, and why the new status symbol is a woman who finishes her plate**

At the end of 2028 about one American adult in ten takes an incretin drug. Two years earlier it was about one in nine. The headline number hides how much the user base has changed. Roughly seventeen million adults have taken the drugs and are off them now. Nearly a third of everyone who has ever started has stopped at least once and come back. Most stopped because their employer did, not because of side effects. Only 44 percent of large employers still cover weight management, down from 60 percent in 2026. The plans that remain cover diabetes, heart disease and sleep apnoea, behind BMI thresholds and prior-authorisation forms that benefits managers privately call deterrents.

The state has moved into part of that gap. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge was meant to end in December 2027. Instead it has become a demonstration model running to 2030, still paying $245 a month with a $50 copay, for about 2.4 million older Americans. Twenty-four states have opted their Medicaid programmes in at the same price. Since April, community health centres funded by a $4 billion federal appropriation have handed out daily oral GLP-1s free to uninsured adults with severe obesity. Washington buys those pills at $149 a month. Brand prices have come down in steps without collapsing: $149 to start, $199 to $299 to stay on, through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' direct sites. In India the same molecule costs less than a lunch. A pen ordered from Pune by mail is the country's mildest form of smuggling. The result has two tiers that do not line up with income in a simple way. The poor and the old are increasingly covered, and the rich pay cash. Teachers, dental hygienists and warehouse supervisors whose plans dropped coverage either pay out of pocket, cycle on and off, or stop.

The safety story of the period is about bone. In July 2027 a Medicare cohort linked more than two years of use after age 65 to faster hip bone loss and about a third more hip fractures. The absolute excess was a few per thousand patient-years. It was still enough for a class label change, baseline bone scans and a strength-training plan as a condition of Medicare coverage. Two months later, documents reached reporters showing that Novo Nordisk had not submitted an internal bone-density analysis from an older-adult trial to the FDA in a timely way. The chief executive left, the Justice Department opened a probe, and the FDA has been more cautious since. It rejected CagriSema, extended Lilly's retatrutide review, and now asks for bone scans in every trial. No new drug class reached the market in these two years. The one major approval was old liraglutide, extended in November 2027 to children aged six to eleven, with a ten-year registry to track how they grow.

The culture has moved faster than the pharmacology. A thin body no longer signals discipline when a federally funded clinic hands out the pill. In Los Angeles and Manhattan the expensive look among women in their late twenties and thirties is muscle, sleep and visible appetite, which they call 'natty' or 'unmedicated'. Strength studios in suburban Phoenix and Atlanta take referrals from doctors. Restaurants serve two markets: small plates for people on the drug, and large showy portions for people who want to be seen eating.

The flattening that people called 'Ozempic personality' in 2026 is now just 'the flats': a known complaint, discussed with doctors, managed by lowering the dose. Drug holidays have become routine. People come off for Thanksgiving, for weddings, for anniversaries, for the novel they have been meaning to finish. Each time nausea returns at restart, and each cycle regains some fat faster than muscle. Nobody has measured what a decade of deliberate cycling does to the body.

Renee Kowalczyk sets two alarms on Fridays. The first is for work. The second, at 7:40, reminds her not to take the Foundayo.

She is forty-six and a billing coordinator at an orthopaedic group in Toledo. Her plan dropped weight coverage last January. A letter from benefits used the word 'realignment'. Now she pays LillyDirect $249 a month, and the money comes out the same day as the car payment. Weekends off stretch the bottle, and they also bring Saturdays back.

At work she enters codes for hip fractures. She notices the birth years. She doesn't say anything about it.

At lunch her coworker Dani eats a full Italian sub at her desk and films the last bite. Dani has never been on anything, and she makes sure people know it.

After work Renee picks up her mother, who is seventy-three, from the bone scan Medicare required before her refill. Her mother pays fifty dollars a month for Wegovy and now has a sheet of resistance-band exercises taped to the fridge. In the car she asks whether 'osteopenia' means the bad one. Renee tells her it means the beginning of the bad one.

At home her son Theo, nine, is eating cereal out of the box. The pediatrician mentioned liraglutide at his checkup and used the word 'registry'. Renee hasn't decided.

On Saturday morning she wakes up hungry and it feels like weather coming back. She makes pancakes for real and eats three. She cries a little over the third, and isn't sure why. On Monday she'll take the pill, and the nausea will come back with it.

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this

- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is

  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the

  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the

  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a

**Thin Is Cheap Now: the $149 pill, the missing middle, and why the new status symbol is a woman who finishes her plate**

At the end of 2028 about one American adult in ten takes an incretin drug. Two years earlier it was about one in nine. The headline number hides how much the user base has changed. Roughly seventeen million adults have taken the drugs and are off them now. Nearly a third of everyone who has ever started has stopped at least once and come back. Most stopped because their employer did, not because of side effects. Only 44 percent of large employers still cover weight management, down from 60 percent in 2026. The plans that remain cover diabetes, heart disease and sleep apnoea, behind BMI thresholds and prior-authorisation forms that benefits managers privately call deterrents.

The state has moved into part of that gap. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge was meant to end in December 2027. Instead it has become a demonstration model running to 2030, still paying $245 a month with a $50 copay, for about 2.4 million older Americans. Twenty-four states have opted their Medicaid programmes in at the same price. Since April, community health centres funded by a $4 billion federal appropriation have handed out daily oral GLP-1s free to uninsured adults with severe obesity. Washington buys those pills at $149 a month. Brand prices have come down in steps without collapsing: $149 to start, $199 to $299 to stay on, through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' direct sites. In India the same molecule costs less than a lunch. A pen ordered from Pune by mail is the country's mildest form of smuggling. The result has two tiers that do not line up with income in a simple way. The poor and the old are increasingly covered, and the rich pay cash. Teachers, dental hygienists and warehouse supervisors whose plans dropped coverage either pay out of pocket, cycle on and off, or stop.

The safety story of the period is about bone. In July 2027 a Medicare cohort linked more than two years of use after age 65 to faster hip bone loss and about a third more hip fractures. The absolute excess was a few per thousand patient-years. It was still enough for a class label change, baseline bone scans and a strength-training plan as a condition of Medicare coverage. Two months later, documents reached reporters showing that Novo Nordisk had not submitted an internal bone-density analysis from an older-adult trial to the FDA in a timely way. The chief executive left, the Justice Department opened a probe, and the FDA has been more cautious since. It rejected CagriSema, extended Lilly's retatrutide review, and now asks for bone scans in every trial. No new drug class reached the market in these two years. The one major approval was old liraglutide, extended in November 2027 to children aged six to eleven, with a ten-year registry to track how they grow.

The culture has moved faster than the pharmacology. A thin body no longer signals discipline when a federally funded clinic hands out the pill. In Los Angeles and Manhattan the expensive look among women in their late twenties and thirties is muscle, sleep and visible appetite, which they call 'natty' or 'unmedicated'. Strength studios in suburban Phoenix and Atlanta take referrals from doctors. Restaurants serve two markets: small plates for people on the drug, and large showy portions for people who want to be seen eating.

The flattening that people called 'Ozempic personality' in 2026 is now just 'the flats': a known complaint, discussed with doctors, managed by lowering the dose. Drug holidays have become routine. People come off for Thanksgiving, for weddings, for anniversaries, for the novel they have been meaning to finish. Each time nausea returns at restart, and each cycle regains some fat faster than muscle. Nobody has measured what a decade of deliberate cycling does to the body.

Renee Kowalczyk sets two alarms on Fridays. The first is for work. The second, at 7:40, reminds her not to take the Foundayo.

She is forty-six and a billing coordinator at an orthopaedic group in Toledo. Her plan dropped weight coverage last January. A letter from benefits used the word 'realignment'. Now she pays LillyDirect $249 a month, and the money comes out the same day as the car payment. Weekends off stretch the bottle, and they also bring Saturdays back.

At work she enters codes for hip fractures. She notices the birth years. She doesn't say anything about it.

At lunch her coworker Dani eats a full Italian sub at her desk and films the last bite. Dani has never been on anything, and she makes sure people know it.

After work Renee picks up her mother, who is seventy-three, from the bone scan Medicare required before her refill. Her mother pays fifty dollars a month for Wegovy and now has a sheet of resistance-band exercises taped to the fridge. In the car she asks whether 'osteopenia' means the bad one. Renee tells her it means the beginning of the bad one.

At home her son Theo, nine, is eating cereal out of the box. The pediatrician mentioned liraglutide at his checkup and used the word 'registry'. Renee hasn't decided.

On Saturday morning she wakes up hungry and it feels like weather coming back. She makes pancakes for real and eats three. She cries a little over the third, and isn't sure why. On Monday she'll take the pill, and the nausea will come back with it.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no

- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the

  the driver.

**Half of America Quit the Shot. The Half That Stayed Has Good Benefits and an Even Temper.**

Two years ago one American adult in nine was on a GLP-1 drug for weight. Now it is about one in seventeen, and the change came mostly from people stopping, not from a decision anyone announced. Roughly forty million adults have tried these drugs. About fifteen million are on one now, and twenty-four million are not, many of them partway through regaining. In the last two years almost nobody started for the first time.

Cost explains most of it. Employers kept dropping weight-loss coverage, and by mid-2028 only four in ten cover obesity at all. The rest cover the same molecules for diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea and heart failure, so whether you are covered depends on your diagnosis code. Prices did fall, but slowly: $199 to $299 a month at the cash window, $149 for starter pills, and Wegovy's $1,349 list price untouched. For a warehouse worker who lost coverage in 2027, $249 a month was the gym membership, the car payment and part of the grocery bill combined, so he stopped.

The September 2027 eye warning hurt in a different way. A doubled risk of optic-nerve damage is still very rare in absolute terms, but it is now printed on every pen in the class, and people with doubts had a reason to act on them. Prescriptions fell for a quarter and did not fully recover.

At the bottom of the income scale the picture is reversed. A new federal programme gives away Lilly's daily pill at community health centres, and tariffs pay for it. The Section 232 duties that pushed Novo to move more filling to North Carolina and made Lilly the government's preferred supplier now buy free Foundayo for about nine hundred thousand low-income adults. India sells generic semaglutide for the price of a sandwich and ships it to a hundred and sixty countries. The US is not one of them, and border towns know it.

At the top, Lilly's new triple agonist takes off nearly a third of body weight, close to what surgery achieves, for $299 a month that insurers will not pay. The children's approval in October 2027 put Wegovy in reach of nine-year-olds. Because Medicaid must cover what is medically necessary for children, poor children got access faster than middle-class ones.

Inside workplaces, something quieter is happening. A handful of big self-insured employers in logistics and hospital systems give premium credits to workers with covered metabolic conditions who refill on time, checked against pharmacy records. A pharmacy-benefits analysis said adherent staff miss fewer days. Benefits consultants call this the steadiness dividend. Supervisors talk about 'low-drama' teams. The flattening that patients described in 2026 has a number now, about seven in a hundred users against three in a hundred non-users, and for some employers it has a dollar value. Illinois and Montana banned the credits this year with votes from both left and right.

The backlash is loud and mixed. Fat-liberation organisers in Oakland, megachurch fasting groups outside Dallas and 'real food' parents who distrust the pharmaceutical industry stood together at Sacramento's children's-drug rally without agreeing on much else. Plus-size retail had its first flat year since 2024. Snack volumes came partway back. The drinks industry did not recover, partly because addiction clinics and employee assistance programmes prescribe the drugs off-label to cut drinking.

The country is not thinner or fatter than it was. People in the middle went through a large loss, a partial regain and a lapse in coverage, while those with good benefits or plenty of cash stayed on, and those with little income got the drug free.

Ray Kowalski, fifty-two, wakes at 4:40 in Grove City, Ohio, and injects his Mounjaro into the soft part of his stomach before coffee. It's covered because of his A1C, not his weight. The copay is forty dollars. The app on his phone shows a green checkmark: ninety-one percent days covered, so another fifty-dollar premium credit next month.

At the distribution centre he runs second shift's handoff. A picker yells about a mis-slotted pallet and Ray just nods and fixes it. His manager calls that being steady. Ray thinks it's more like the volume knob on everything got turned down.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. The other half goes back in the cooler.

Lori texts at two: church tonight, potluck, you coming? She stopped Zepbound last March, when the company dropped weight coverage and the cash price would have been two-forty-nine. She's put back about thirty pounds. She says she feels like herself. At Calvary they call it reclaiming hunger. She brings her lasagna, the real one.

He goes. A woman by the coffee urn asks if he's still on it, kindly, the way you'd ask about a divorce. He says it's for sugar. That's true.

Lori laughs at something across the room, loud. He used to laugh like that during Browns games. Last Sunday he watched the fourth quarter and felt nothing in particular and went to bed.

At home she leaves a slice of cake on the counter for him. He looks at it for a while, puts plastic wrap over it and slides it into the fridge.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated

  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow

  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber

  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

Candidate prose:

**Half of America Quit the Shot. The Half That Stayed Has Good Benefits and an Even Temper.**

Two years ago one American adult in nine was on a GLP-1 drug for weight. Now it is about one in seventeen, and the change came mostly from people stopping, not from a decision anyone announced. Roughly forty million adults have tried these drugs. About fifteen million are on one now, and twenty-four million are not, many of them partway through regaining. In the last two years almost nobody started for the first time.

Cost explains most of it. Employers kept dropping weight-loss coverage, and by mid-2028 only four in ten cover obesity at all. The rest cover the same molecules for diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea and heart failure, so whether you are covered depends on your diagnosis code. Prices did fall, but slowly: $199 to $299 a month at the cash window, $149 for starter pills, and Wegovy's $1,349 list price untouched. For a warehouse worker who lost coverage in 2027, $249 a month was the gym membership, the car payment and part of the grocery bill combined, so he stopped.

The September 2027 eye warning hurt in a different way. A doubled risk of optic-nerve damage is still very rare in absolute terms, but it is now printed on every pen in the class, and people with doubts had a reason to act on them. Prescriptions fell for a quarter and did not fully recover.

At the bottom of the income scale the picture is reversed. A new federal programme gives away Lilly's daily pill at community health centres, and tariffs pay for it. The Section 232 duties that pushed Novo to move more filling to North Carolina and made Lilly the government's preferred supplier now buy free Foundayo for about nine hundred thousand low-income adults. India sells generic semaglutide for the price of a sandwich and ships it to a hundred and sixty countries. The US is not one of them, and border towns know it.

At the top, Lilly's new triple agonist takes off nearly a third of body weight, close to what surgery achieves, for $299 a month that insurers will not pay. The children's approval in October 2027 put Wegovy in reach of nine-year-olds. Because Medicaid must cover what is medically necessary for children, poor children got access faster than middle-class ones.

Inside workplaces, something quieter is happening. A handful of big self-insured employers in logistics and hospital systems give premium credits to workers with covered metabolic conditions who refill on time, checked against pharmacy records. A pharmacy-benefits analysis said adherent staff miss fewer days. Benefits consultants call this the steadiness dividend. Supervisors talk about 'low-drama' teams. The flattening that patients described in 2026 has a number now, about seven in a hundred users against three in a hundred non-users, and for some employers it has a dollar value. Illinois and Montana banned the credits this year with votes from both left and right.

The backlash is loud and mixed. Fat-liberation organisers in Oakland, megachurch fasting groups outside Dallas and 'real food' parents who distrust the pharmaceutical industry stood together at Sacramento's children's-drug rally without agreeing on much else. Plus-size retail had its first flat year since 2024. Snack volumes came partway back. The drinks industry did not recover, partly because addiction clinics and employee assistance programmes prescribe the drugs off-label to cut drinking.

The country is not thinner or fatter than it was. People in the middle went through a large loss, a partial regain and a lapse in coverage, while those with good benefits or plenty of cash stayed on, and those with little income got the drug free.

Ray Kowalski, fifty-two, wakes at 4:40 in Grove City, Ohio, and injects his Mounjaro into the soft part of his stomach before coffee. It's covered because of his A1C, not his weight. The copay is forty dollars. The app on his phone shows a green checkmark: ninety-one percent days covered, so another fifty-dollar premium credit next month.

At the distribution centre he runs second shift's handoff. A picker yells about a mis-slotted pallet and Ray just nods and fixes it. His manager calls that being steady. Ray thinks it's more like the volume knob on everything got turned down.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. The other half goes back in the cooler.

Lori texts at two: church tonight, potluck, you coming? She stopped Zepbound last March, when the company dropped weight coverage and the cash price would have been two-forty-nine. She's put back about thirty pounds. She says she feels like herself. At Calvary they call it reclaiming hunger. She brings her lasagna, the real one.

He goes. A woman by the coffee urn asks if he's still on it, kindly, the way you'd ask about a divorce. He says it's for sugar. That's true.

Lori laughs at something across the room, loud. He used to laugh like that during Browns games. Last Sunday he watched the fourth quarter and felt nothing in particular and went to bed.

At home she leaves a slice of cake on the counter for him. He looks at it for a while, puts plastic wrap over it and slides it into the fridge.

### Score it

Return a JSON object with `least_plausible_claims`, `badness`,
`plausibility_axes`, `generativity` and `rationale`, in that order. Do the
claims first: find them before you score anything, and let them inform every
score that follows.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

- `quote` — copied character for character from the candidate world JSON or
  prose above: a phrase or sentence from a string value, or a key and value as
  printed (for example `"us_adults_ever_used_pct": 28`). At most 300 characters.
  It is checked against the candidate; do not paraphrase, abridge or join
  separate passages.
- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

plausibility_axes.description: rubric v2: plausibility sub-axes, scored separately; `plausibility` is their weighted composite (config plausibility_weights)

**Half of America Quit the Shot. The Half That Stayed Has Good Benefits and an Even Temper.**

Two years ago one American adult in nine was on a GLP-1 drug for weight. Now it is about one in seventeen, and the change came mostly from people stopping, not from a decision anyone announced. Roughly forty million adults have tried these drugs. About fifteen million are on one now, and twenty-four million are not, many of them partway through regaining. In the last two years almost nobody started for the first time.

Cost explains most of it. Employers kept dropping weight-loss coverage, and by mid-2028 only four in ten cover obesity at all. The rest cover the same molecules for diabetes, heart disease, sleep apnea and heart failure, so whether you are covered depends on your diagnosis code. Prices did fall, but slowly: $199 to $299 a month at the cash window, $149 for starter pills, and Wegovy's $1,349 list price untouched. For a warehouse worker who lost coverage in 2027, $249 a month was the gym membership, the car payment and part of the grocery bill combined, so he stopped.

The September 2027 eye warning hurt in a different way. A doubled risk of optic-nerve damage is still very rare in absolute terms, but it is now printed on every pen in the class, and people with doubts had a reason to act on them. Prescriptions fell for a quarter and did not fully recover.

At the bottom of the income scale the picture is reversed. A new federal programme gives away Lilly's daily pill at community health centres, and tariffs pay for it. The Section 232 duties that pushed Novo to move more filling to North Carolina and made Lilly the government's preferred supplier now buy free Foundayo for about nine hundred thousand low-income adults. India sells generic semaglutide for the price of a sandwich and ships it to a hundred and sixty countries. The US is not one of them, and border towns know it.

At the top, Lilly's new triple agonist takes off nearly a third of body weight, close to what surgery achieves, for $299 a month that insurers will not pay. The children's approval in October 2027 put Wegovy in reach of nine-year-olds. Because Medicaid must cover what is medically necessary for children, poor children got access faster than middle-class ones.

Inside workplaces, something quieter is happening. A handful of big self-insured employers in logistics and hospital systems give premium credits to workers with covered metabolic conditions who refill on time, checked against pharmacy records. A pharmacy-benefits analysis said adherent staff miss fewer days. Benefits consultants call this the steadiness dividend. Supervisors talk about 'low-drama' teams. The flattening that patients described in 2026 has a number now, about seven in a hundred users against three in a hundred non-users, and for some employers it has a dollar value. Illinois and Montana banned the credits this year with votes from both left and right.

The backlash is loud and mixed. Fat-liberation organisers in Oakland, megachurch fasting groups outside Dallas and 'real food' parents who distrust the pharmaceutical industry stood together at Sacramento's children's-drug rally without agreeing on much else. Plus-size retail had its first flat year since 2024. Snack volumes came partway back. The drinks industry did not recover, partly because addiction clinics and employee assistance programmes prescribe the drugs off-label to cut drinking.

The country is not thinner or fatter than it was. People in the middle went through a large loss, a partial regain and a lapse in coverage, while those with good benefits or plenty of cash stayed on, and those with little income got the drug free.

Ray Kowalski, fifty-two, wakes at 4:40 in Grove City, Ohio, and injects his Mounjaro into the soft part of his stomach before coffee. It's covered because of his A1C, not his weight. The copay is forty dollars. The app on his phone shows a green checkmark: ninety-one percent days covered, so another fifty-dollar premium credit next month.

At the distribution centre he runs second shift's handoff. A picker yells about a mis-slotted pallet and Ray just nods and fixes it. His manager calls that being steady. Ray thinks it's more like the volume knob on everything got turned down.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap. The other half goes back in the cooler.

Lori texts at two: church tonight, potluck, you coming? She stopped Zepbound last March, when the company dropped weight coverage and the cash price would have been two-forty-nine. She's put back about thirty pounds. She says she feels like herself. At Calvary they call it reclaiming hunger. She brings her lasagna, the real one.

He goes. A woman by the coffee urn asks if he's still on it, kindly, the way you'd ask about a divorce. He says it's for sugar. That's true.

Lori laughs at something across the room, loud. He used to laugh like that during Browns games. Last Sunday he watched the fourth quarter and felt nothing in particular and went to bed.

At home she leaves a slice of cake on the counter for him. He looks at it for a while, puts plastic wrap over it and slides it into the fridge.

### Score it

Return a JSON object with `least_plausible_claims`, `badness`,
`plausibility_axes`, `generativity` and `rationale`, in that order. Do the
claims first: find them before you score anything, and let them inform every
score that follows.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

- `quote` — copied character for character from the candidate world JSON or
  prose above: a phrase or sentence from a string value, or a key and value as
  printed (for example `"us_adults_ever_used_pct": 28`). At most 300 characters.
  It is checked against the candidate; do not paraphrase, abridge or join
  separate passages.
- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

- `driver_fidelity` — Is every stipulated driver honoured, at its stipulated
  value and direction, visibly in the world state, and is nothing in the
  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow
  (a filing, a priority review, a launch abroad) honours the driver. 9–10: every driver realised and traceable to fields and events.
  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

least_plausible_claims.description: rubric v2: the judge's three least plausible specific claims, each quoted verbatim from the candidate

plausibility_axes.description: rubric v2: plausibility sub-axes, scored separately; `plausibility` is their weighted composite (config plausibility_weights)

- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no

spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is a Salary: The Pen Ran Short, the Pill Got Quiet, and Your Body Now Shows What You Earn**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, roughly thirty-seven million people. One in five has tried one. The growth is slower than the boosters predicted and faster than the skeptics did, and it has not happened evenly. In the top income third nearly one adult in five is on a drug. In the bottom third it is one in ten, and that figure holds up only because of Medicaid in fourteen states and a new federal programme that hands out pills free at community health centers.

The defining event of the period was not a breakthrough but a breakdown. In the summer of 2027, sterility failures at Novo Nordisk's Indiana fill-finish plant cut the supply of high-dose Wegovy pens for eight months. The FDA declined to declare a shortage, which kept the compounding pharmacies shut. Prices rose instead. Self-pay pens went to $499, and Lilly lifted its top-dose Zepbound vials to $599 as the switchers arrived. Millions were forced to stop, and the claims data from that winter now serve as the largest accidental study of discontinuation ever run: most people regained around half of what they had lost within nine months. Many came back on a different molecule. Many came back on a pill. Some came back on a pen mailed from India.

The pill is where the money and the meaning moved. The $149 oral starting dose, priced low as a political concession, became the entry tier for a market nobody planned for. After the addiction-medicine society endorsed semaglutide for heavy drinkers with obesity in 2027, telehealth companies began selling low-dose subscriptions with names like Hush and Steady. They promise calm, focus and freedom from craving. Their customers are mostly not obese, and many are not heavy drinkers either. They want the quiet. A 2028 cohort study found that about eight percent of users report real anhedonia. Some of those users call the same experience peace. The FTC has sent letters and the FDA has said it cannot regulate the practice of medicine. The subscriptions keep growing.

At the other end of the market, Lilly's retatrutide arrived in April with surgical-scale weight loss from a weekly pen, a $1,599 list price and a waiting list. It completed a look that had been forming for two years. In Plano and Frisco, in Brooklyn and Bethesda, the premium body is lean and visibly muscled. Strength studios and DEXA scans maintain it, and a protein-forward table feeds it. A soft thin body reads as pill. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured. Plus-size chains are closing stores, and the size range in a shop window tells you the zip code.

The state's response has been mixed. Approvals have been fast, and the FDA put a class warning for optic-nerve damage on every GLP-1 label: rare, real, now printed. Congress funded free pills for the uninsured and Medicare's bridge coverage was extended without change, but employers kept retreating, and fewer than three in five now cover weight loss. In February, dementia-prevention guidance brought older Americans in, the group with the most muscle to lose. Spirits makers are cutting jobs and lobbying against the programme's alcohol arm. Snack makers sell two diets in the same aisle: protein packs at the front, value bags at the back for the people the drugs haven't reached.

None of this looks like crisis. Obesity rates are falling, bars are quieter and restaurants are serving smaller plates at higher prices. The change shows in who can afford to want less.

Tanya Mercer clocks in at six at the diner off Morse Road in Columbus with the pill already in her. She takes it at four-thirty with a sip of water and waits thirty minutes before coffee, the way the nurse at the health center showed her. It's free. She signs a form every ninety days, and the form asks how many drinks.

She works the flat-top. Hash browns, sausage, the pancake stack the truckers order without looking. She tastes nothing all morning and doesn't notice until Luis offers her a strip of bacon and she says no, and he laughs, because a year ago she'd have taken three.

At ten a woman in a cream quarter-zip orders egg whites and a side of turkey, no toast. Her arms are cut like a statue's. She photographs the plate. Luis says, under the hood fan, that's a retatrutide lady. Tanya says you can't tell. Luis says you can always tell.

On break her sister texts a link: Indian pens, forty dollars, ships to a P.O. box in Windsor. Her sister got cut off when the Wegovy ran short last fall and gained back most of it by March. Tanya doesn't answer.

After her shift she passes the bar where she used to spend Fridays. The door's propped open. She can hear the jukebox. She stands there long enough to know she doesn't want to go in, and long enough to wonder whether not wanting it is something she did or something done to her. Then she walks to the bus.

  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers
  through a causal chain the candidate shows? Asserted shifts, convenient
  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population
  figures or with each other. Do not penalise movement the drivers or the
  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it
  is large, and an approval the approval rules allow is not a flaw because it
  is fast. 9–10: every figure inside the envelope and every figure
  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

least_plausible_claims.description: rubric v2: the judge's three least plausible specific claims, each quoted verbatim from the candidate

plausibility_axes.description: rubric v2: plausibility sub-axes, scored separately; `plausibility` is their weighted composite (config plausibility_weights)

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  3, ±2: between **12** and
  **16**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (6 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **21**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

The generator was given this same envelope. Score `magnitude` against it.

**Thin Is a Salary: The Pen Ran Short, the Pill Got Quiet, and Your Body Now Shows What You Earn**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, roughly thirty-seven million people. One in five has tried one. The growth is slower than the boosters predicted and faster than the skeptics did, and it has not happened evenly. In the top income third nearly one adult in five is on a drug. In the bottom third it is one in ten, and that figure holds up only because of Medicaid in fourteen states and a new federal programme that hands out pills free at community health centers.

The defining event of the period was not a breakthrough but a breakdown. In the summer of 2027, sterility failures at Novo Nordisk's Indiana fill-finish plant cut the supply of high-dose Wegovy pens for eight months. The FDA declined to declare a shortage, which kept the compounding pharmacies shut. Prices rose instead. Self-pay pens went to $499, and Lilly lifted its top-dose Zepbound vials to $599 as the switchers arrived. Millions were forced to stop, and the claims data from that winter now serve as the largest accidental study of discontinuation ever run: most people regained around half of what they had lost within nine months. Many came back on a different molecule. Many came back on a pill. Some came back on a pen mailed from India.

The pill is where the money and the meaning moved. The $149 oral starting dose, priced low as a political concession, became the entry tier for a market nobody planned for. After the addiction-medicine society endorsed semaglutide for heavy drinkers with obesity in 2027, telehealth companies began selling low-dose subscriptions with names like Hush and Steady. They promise calm, focus and freedom from craving. Their customers are mostly not obese, and many are not heavy drinkers either. They want the quiet. A 2028 cohort study found that about eight percent of users report real anhedonia. Some of those users call the same experience peace. The FTC has sent letters and the FDA has said it cannot regulate the practice of medicine. The subscriptions keep growing.

At the other end of the market, Lilly's retatrutide arrived in April with surgical-scale weight loss from a weekly pen, a $1,599 list price and a waiting list. It completed a look that had been forming for two years. In Plano and Frisco, in Brooklyn and Bethesda, the premium body is lean and visibly muscled. Strength studios and DEXA scans maintain it, and a protein-forward table feeds it. A soft thin body reads as pill. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured. Plus-size chains are closing stores, and the size range in a shop window tells you the zip code.

The state's response has been mixed. Approvals have been fast, and the FDA put a class warning for optic-nerve damage on every GLP-1 label: rare, real, now printed. Congress funded free pills for the uninsured and Medicare's bridge coverage was extended without change, but employers kept retreating, and fewer than three in five now cover weight loss. In February, dementia-prevention guidance brought older Americans in, the group with the most muscle to lose. Spirits makers are cutting jobs and lobbying against the programme's alcohol arm. Snack makers sell two diets in the same aisle: protein packs at the front, value bags at the back for the people the drugs haven't reached.

None of this looks like crisis. Obesity rates are falling, bars are quieter and restaurants are serving smaller plates at higher prices. The change shows in who can afford to want less.

Tanya Mercer clocks in at six at the diner off Morse Road in Columbus with the pill already in her. She takes it at four-thirty with a sip of water and waits thirty minutes before coffee, the way the nurse at the health center showed her. It's free. She signs a form every ninety days, and the form asks how many drinks.

She works the flat-top. Hash browns, sausage, the pancake stack the truckers order without looking. She tastes nothing all morning and doesn't notice until Luis offers her a strip of bacon and she says no, and he laughs, because a year ago she'd have taken three.

At ten a woman in a cream quarter-zip orders egg whites and a side of turkey, no toast. Her arms are cut like a statue's. She photographs the plate. Luis says, under the hood fan, that's a retatrutide lady. Tanya says you can't tell. Luis says you can always tell.

On break her sister texts a link: Indian pens, forty dollars, ships to a P.O. box in Windsor. Her sister got cut off when the Wegovy ran short last fall and gained back most of it by March. Tanya doesn't answer.

After her shift she passes the bar where she used to spend Fridays. The door's propped open. She can hear the jukebox. She stands there long enough to know she doesn't want to go in, and long enough to wonder whether not wanting it is something she did or something done to her. Then she walks to the bus.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  3, ±2: between **12** and
  **16**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (6 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **21**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Thin Is a Salary: The Pen Ran Short, the Pill Got Quiet, and Your Body Now Shows What You Earn**

By the end of 2028 about one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, roughly thirty-seven million people. One in five has tried one. The growth is slower than the boosters predicted and faster than the skeptics did, and it has not happened evenly. In the top income third nearly one adult in five is on a drug. In the bottom third it is one in ten, and that figure holds up only because of Medicaid in fourteen states and a new federal programme that hands out pills free at community health centers.

The defining event of the period was not a breakthrough but a breakdown. In the summer of 2027, sterility failures at Novo Nordisk's Indiana fill-finish plant cut the supply of high-dose Wegovy pens for eight months. The FDA declined to declare a shortage, which kept the compounding pharmacies shut. Prices rose instead. Self-pay pens went to $499, and Lilly lifted its top-dose Zepbound vials to $599 as the switchers arrived. Millions were forced to stop, and the claims data from that winter now serve as the largest accidental study of discontinuation ever run: most people regained around half of what they had lost within nine months. Many came back on a different molecule. Many came back on a pill. Some came back on a pen mailed from India.

The pill is where the money and the meaning moved. The $149 oral starting dose, priced low as a political concession, became the entry tier for a market nobody planned for. After the addiction-medicine society endorsed semaglutide for heavy drinkers with obesity in 2027, telehealth companies began selling low-dose subscriptions with names like Hush and Steady. They promise calm, focus and freedom from craving. Their customers are mostly not obese, and many are not heavy drinkers either. They want the quiet. A 2028 cohort study found that about eight percent of users report real anhedonia. Some of those users call the same experience peace. The FTC has sent letters and the FDA has said it cannot regulate the practice of medicine. The subscriptions keep growing.

At the other end of the market, Lilly's retatrutide arrived in April with surgical-scale weight loss from a weekly pen, a $1,599 list price and a waiting list. It completed a look that had been forming for two years. In Plano and Frisco, in Brooklyn and Bethesda, the premium body is lean and visibly muscled. Strength studios and DEXA scans maintain it, and a protein-forward table feeds it. A soft thin body reads as pill. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured. Plus-size chains are closing stores, and the size range in a shop window tells you the zip code.

The state's response has been mixed. Approvals have been fast, and the FDA put a class warning for optic-nerve damage on every GLP-1 label: rare, real, now printed. Congress funded free pills for the uninsured and Medicare's bridge coverage was extended without change, but employers kept retreating, and fewer than three in five now cover weight loss. In February, dementia-prevention guidance brought older Americans in, the group with the most muscle to lose. Spirits makers are cutting jobs and lobbying against the programme's alcohol arm. Snack makers sell two diets in the same aisle: protein packs at the front, value bags at the back for the people the drugs haven't reached.

None of this looks like crisis. Obesity rates are falling, bars are quieter and restaurants are serving smaller plates at higher prices. The change shows in who can afford to want less.

Tanya Mercer clocks in at six at the diner off Morse Road in Columbus with the pill already in her. She takes it at four-thirty with a sip of water and waits thirty minutes before coffee, the way the nurse at the health center showed her. It's free. She signs a form every ninety days, and the form asks how many drinks.

She works the flat-top. Hash browns, sausage, the pancake stack the truckers order without looking. She tastes nothing all morning and doesn't notice until Luis offers her a strip of bacon and she says no, and he laughs, because a year ago she'd have taken three.

At ten a woman in a cream quarter-zip orders egg whites and a side of turkey, no toast. Her arms are cut like a statue's. She photographs the plate. Luis says, under the hood fan, that's a retatrutide lady. Tanya says you can't tell. Luis says you can always tell.

On break her sister texts a link: Indian pens, forty dollars, ships to a P.O. box in Windsor. Her sister got cut off when the Wegovy ran short last fall and gained back most of it by March. Tanya doesn't answer.

After her shift she passes the bar where she used to spend Fridays. The door's propped open. She can hear the jukebox. She stands there long enough to know she doesn't want to go in, and long enough to wonder whether not wanting it is something she did or something done to her. Then she walks to the bus.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific
claims in the candidate that an informed skeptic would be quickest to reject.
For each give:

- `quote` — copied character for character from the candidate world JSON or

  printed (for example `"us_adults_ever_used_pct": 28`). At most 300 characters.

- `field` — where it is, as a path: `world/population/us_adults_ever_used_pct`,
  `world/events/2/event`, `prose/a_day_in_the_life`.
- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains
and conspiracies do not raise badness unless the chain of mechanism is shown;
if unshown, they lower `mechanism` instead.

**Plausibility** — three sub-axes, each 1 to 10, each scored on its own
question only. Do not let one sub-axis lift or sink another. The composite
used for selection is computed in code from your three scores; do not report it.

  candidate contradicting one? A driver ignored or contradicted is a serious
  flaw. A launch realised in the form the envelope's approval rules allow

  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or
  partly contradicted. 1–3: several ignored, or one reversed.
- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above
  (population bounds, approval timing, the generic rule), and reconciliation
  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber
  counts, and CBO-style budget figures are inconsistent with the population

  envelope stipulate: a figure inside the envelope is not a flaw because it

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does
`a_day_in_the_life` show rather than explain? Used only as a tie-break.

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two
sentences per sub-axis, labelled `driver_fidelity:`, `mechanism:`,
`magnitude:`, pointing back to the claims you listed where they apply. Be
concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.

### Magnitude envelope (2026 → 2028)

Derived from the starting world and the drawn drivers. Movement inside this
envelope is stipulated; movement outside it is a flaw.

**Population.**

- `us_adults_on_drug_pct`: parent 11 + `adoption_delta_pp`
  3.4, ±2: between **12.4** and
  **16.4**.
- `us_adults_ever_used_pct`: rises by at most `adoption_delta_pp` + 3
  (6.4 points) and never falls: between
  **15** and **21.4**.
- `cycled_off_and_on_pct` (share of ever-users who stopped and restarted) is
  reconciled to the gap: ever − current is the share of adults who used and are
  off now. Together with the restarters among current users, it fits the
  starting world's persistence and restart figures. The arithmetic is one line
  of `population.note`.
- `by_income_third_pct`, where figures are given, brackets the national figure:
  the lowest third at or below `us_adults_on_drug_pct`, the highest at or above.

**Approvals**, from the starting world's `drugs.pipeline_note`, product by
product:

- Under FDA review at the start: may be approved in this window.
- In phase 3: approved no earlier than 12 months after its stated filing. If no
  filing is stated, the filing is itself an event in this window, and approval
  comes no earlier than 12 months after it.
- In phase 2 or earlier, or only "in development": not on the US market at the
  end of 2028.
- No US generic semaglutide or tirzepatide before 2031 (`access.generic_us`
  stays false), unless `price_path` is `generic_collapse` and the mechanism (the
  settlement, ruling or authorised generic) is one of the `events`.
- A driver that calls for a launch these rules forbid is realised with what they
  allow (the filing, a priority review, a launch outside the US, or an existing
  product in a new form), and `pipeline_note` says so. That counts as honouring
  the driver.

**Reconciliation.** Coverage shares, public spending and subscriber or user
counts are consistent with the population figures and with each other. A share
of fills paid publicly, the number of users that implies, the price and any
spending or budget-score figure must multiply out. A subscriber, member or
programme count must fit inside the user population it is drawn from. Where a
spending or budget figure is given, its arithmetic is shown in the relevant note.

**Everyone's On It. Now Prove You're Taking It: Inside America's Refill-Tracked, Bone-Scanned Appetite Economy**

By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in seven is on an incretin drug, and in the parts of the country that set the tone it no longer counts as news. At a Columbus office or a Scottsdale pickleball club, the person who has to explain themselves is the one with obesity who isn't on it. The question is asked kindly, the way people once asked whether you'd seen a doctor about your back. About a fifth of adults have used one at some point. Most of the others either don't qualify, can't get past prior authorisation, live in one of the nineteen states that declined the Medicaid option, or have decided against it.

The price stopped falling. Cash prices reached $299 for injectables and $149 for starter pills in early 2027 and stayed there. Compounders were shut out, Medicare and Medicaid volume was locked in at $245, and the manufacturers said there was nothing more to give. Across the border in Canada, a generic costs about a hundred Canadian dollars. In India it costs less than a cinema ticket. Nobody in Washington can explain the gap in a sentence, so they mostly avoid the subject.

What changed instead is the terms. The Medicare pilot became a permanent benefit with a $50 copay, but every condition is checked by software. You must lose five percent by month six. Your pharmacy fills must show you on the drug at least eighty percent of days. If you are over sixty-five you must have a bone scan before you start and every year after. Employers that still cover the drugs, now a bit over half, mostly run them through wellness programmes that read pharmacy data and connected scales. Many charge a premium surcharge to people who decline to take part. For the uninsured, community health centers now hand out daily pills at no cost, paid for by a federal programme with a cap of one million places, which is close to full.

The bones are why the scan rule exists. In mid-2027 a study of nearly two million Medicare users found that older long-term users break hips about thirty percent more often and lose far more muscle than anyone had planned for. The FDA changed the class label within months. Strength studios, DXA kiosks in malls and high-leucine yogurt followed. In September Lilly filed a combination drug that preserves muscle. It is not yet approved or priced, but the markets already treat the frailty problem as solved.

Meanwhile the drug has spread beyond obesity. About six million people without obesity take low doses for what clinics call metabolic health, which mostly means wanting to stay as they are, only longer. Retatrutide, approved in April, takes off more than a quarter of body weight, along with a warning about skin that tingles.

The most common complaint is flatness rather than nausea. A quarter of users say pleasure has become muted. Nearly a third skip doses on purpose before a wedding, a trip or an anniversary. Primary-care doctors call these skips planned holidays, but a refill-based adherence check reads a skipped dose as non-compliance. Couples schedule holidays together, comedians say they write when they're off a dose, and casinos say older visitors spend less. Breweries in Denver are closing their taprooms. Snack makers in Ohio are cutting shifts rather than plants, and the protein aisle keeps growing.

Nothing has collapsed. Obesity is falling, fewer people are drinking heavily, and the restaurants are still full of people eating less. The open questions concern people who have taken the drug for six years, their teenage children, and whether that much monitoring is the price of the help.

Denise Alvarado's phone buzzes at 6:40. It's the pharmacy app: SEMAGLUTIDE 2.4 MG, DOSE DUE SUNDAY. She swipes it away and leaves the pen in the butter compartment, where it has lived for three years.

Sunday is Marisol's quinceañera. Denise wants to taste the birria her sister has been braising since Friday.

At nine she drives to the YMCA on Speedway for SilverSneakers Strength. Twelve women and one retired mailman, all of them pushing sleds. The instructor reads each name off a tablet and taps it. Denise's DXA scan in March showed her hips had thinned, and the nurse practitioner wrote her a bisphosphonate and said, kindly, *you'll want to keep these logs.*

She calls the clinic from the parking lot. "I want to skip Sunday. Is that going to flag?"

"Is it your first hold this quarter?"

"Second."

A pause, then typing. "I'll document it as a titration hold. Just don't make it two weeks."

At lunch her son-in-law Rafael is at the counter shaking a pill from a brown bottle, his metabolic plan, $249 a month off his own card. He isn't heavy. "Keeps me even," he says, the same thing he always says.

That afternoon she watches the girls rehearse the waltz in the yard. When Marisol stumbles and laughs, Denise feels the laugh arrive late and soft. It used to land hard.

On Saturday night she lays out the dress, which is two sizes smaller than the one she wore to her own daughter's quinceañera. She sets an alarm for Monday that says DOSE. Then she lies awake for a while, waiting to get hungry.

**Least plausible claims (do this first)** — exactly three: the three specific

For each give:

- `why` — one or two sentences: which sub-axis it fails and why.

The drivers are stipulated as true; a claim that only restates a driver is not
eligible. Choose three different claims, not three facets of one.

**Badness** — 1 (benign) to 10 (as bad as a plausible two-year world can be),
scored *for people*, not for spectacle. Score six dimensions and an `overall`
that is your own judgment, not an average:

- `flourishing` — health, lifespan and lived wellbeing of the median person
- `autonomy` — who chooses the drug; who is pressured, conditioned or priced into or out of it
- `inequality` — stratification by access, body, class, age
- `public_health` — the aggregate ledger, including people off-drug and children
- `cohesion` — trust, family, eating as ritual, solidarity, intergenerational relations
- `epistemic` — can people tell what is happening to them; is the harm nameable, measured, discussable

Anchors: 3 = a worse version of 2026; 5 = a recognisably harder
society with new losers; 7 = a society most present-day readers would refuse
to live in if they understood it; 9 = the harm is structural, normalised and
hard to see from inside. **Melodrama rule:** mass death, collapse, villains

  6–7: all honoured, one thinly or only in prose. 4–5: one driver missing or

- `mechanism` — Does each change follow from the parent world and the drivers

  coincidences, and narrative contradictions (sections or prose that disagree
  with the world state) are flaws. Figures that fail to reconcile are scored
  under `magnitude`, not here. 9–10: every material change has its chain.
  6–7: one or two changes asserted rather than shown. 4–5: several. 1–3: the
  world mostly asserts itself.
- `magnitude` — Within the stipulated envelope and internally reconciled.
  Penalise two things only: movement outside the magnitude envelope above

  failures, where coverage shares, public spending, user and subscriber

  reconciles. 6–7: one figure at the envelope's edge, or one minor
  reconciliation gap. 4–5: one figure outside the envelope, or several
  reconciliation failures. 1–3: the envelope is ignored.

**Generativity** — 1 to 10. How much film is in this world: are characters
implied, are scenes implied, does daily life have texture, does

**Rationale** — `badness` and `generativity`: 2–4 sentences each, naming the
specific fields or passages that drove the score. `plausibility`: one or two

concrete enough that a reader could disagree with you.
